speakerposition: topic
maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. EDGAR N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the debate on the address I stated that in my opinion "strong measures" would have to be taken to remedy the evils under which Canada is suffering. I further suggested that the most important of these measures could not be enacted into law or practice unless there was some degree of
cooperation between federal and provincial authorities, and likewise between the various parties and factions in this house.
Some of those measures I propose to expound to-day, realizing of course that they are not all of equal value and importance, and further, that they could not all be put into execution at once. But I sincerely believe that most, if not all, of them are worthy of being considered without bias by every member of this house. I propose to offer them, so far as my temperament permits, in the most lenient and conciliatory manner. If, at times, my words sound harsh in the ears of some of my fellow-members, I pray them in all sincerity to disregard the sound and to consider the intention, which, I assure them, is altogether friendly and conciliatory.
In order to cover the ground, and as well to remain within the rules of this house, I think it proper to resort to a time honoured procedure of the British House of Commons, "that grand inquest of the nation," as it has been called for centuries; and therefore at the end of my remarks I shall move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), in amendment to the motion that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of supply:
That the house, while prepared to grant to His Majesty all necessary supply to carry on the administration of the country, is of the opinion that a special committee of the house should be appointed to inquire into the state of the nation and suggest prompt and effective measures of economic and social reform.
With regard to financial matters proper, I propose to be as short and concise as possible; first, because I have not the slightest pretension to being an expert in such matters, and secondly, because they have been and are daily being discussed in this house in various forms. May I say to the Prime Minister that I quite sympathize with him, in this regard? I read with pleasure and sympathy the remarks he made last night about the same questions coming up over and over again. Of course that is unavoidable; and my only purpose in referring to some of these questions is simply to cover the ground and indicate the action on finance, taxation, trade, and social reform, which I think is imperatively needed.
First-I will not say first in importance, but it is the most obvious factor in the situation-is the debt, federal, provincial, municipal, corporative, individual. Undoubtedly Canada, more perhaps than any other country, is overburdened with debt. Undoubtedly, again, it ought to be the main concern of every government, and I use the word government in

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
the broadest sense to include not only political governments but industrial governments as well, to search unceasingly for some practical means of reducing that burden. Many have been suggested. My friends to the left, on various occasions in years past, and this year again, have suggested what they call the inflation or reflation of money, in order to increase the purchasing power of the masses of the people, and also to enable debtors to pay their debts with less money than they received. I have read much on inflation in theory, and also as applied in various countries of the world. Is it because of the infirmity of my mind, or perhaps because of what my good friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) termed once my infernal French logic? but I have not yet been able quite to agree with my friends to the left, as to the beneficial results of inflation.
When they speak of controlled inflation, well and good; but the experience of the world in the last ten or fifteen years-I might say centuries, because inflation is nothing new: Philip the Fair of France, in the fourteenth century, resorted to inflation in his own way; the French Convention, also, when it created the assignats; that was inflation with a vengeance-long experience and contemporary history teach us that controlled inflation soon becomes uncontrollable inflation.
But what makes me more doubtful still is the obvious fact frequently pointed out by the Prime Minister-and it ought to be obvious to all-that you cannot compare the situation of Canada with that of many other countries which have resorted to inflation. No system of economics can operate in exactly the same way in two or more countries situated in different circumstances. Canada has enormous natural resources to be developed in the future; but, at present, Canada owes not only to her own nationals, as does France for example, apart from her war debts, but we owe also to various countries, and more especially to the United States and England. How would a policy of inflation result in a settlement of our debt to England, on the one hand, and to the United States on the other? Of course, if you could get the British and American governments to maintain equilibrium between their currencies and ours, if you could get our British and American creditors, holders of our bonds, federal, provincial, municipal and railway bonds, to accept payment in terms of our own currency, well and good. But will they?
One of the main reasons given by our friends to the left was that a controlled inflation resulting, iit was said last year, in bring-
ing the Canadian dollar on a par with sterling, would have a tremendously stimulating effect upon the sale of our wheat, for example. If I remember aright, the pound sterling, as compared with our dollar, stood then around S3.50. It has been quoted for some weeks now at $5.10 of our currency; but I have yet to learn, either from the press or from any information given to this house, that the price of our wheat has risen in proportion to the downfall of our dollar. That is what it is; it is not the pound sterling which has gone up, it is our dollar which has gone down. Where is the benefit to the seller of wheat or of any other commodity in an inflation such as we have had?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: Was that not the cause of the rise in the price of wheat last year?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Perhaps it was. I am not conversant with those matters, I am simply suggesting that it has not had all the effects which it was expected it would have.
_ In discussing these questions of currency, inflation and deflation, and later on, taxation, my main concern is for that class of people which is not represented by any party in this house. The lower middle class do not belong to any labour organization, to any farmers' organization, to any manufacturers' association or to any organization of business men or social workers, in the broad sense of the word. They receive very little consideration at the hands of municipal, provincial and federal governments. In this country as in every other country, this class is the mainstay of social order; it is the cement which maintains a certain degree of harmony and conciliation between the various classes of the community. Inflation would ruin most of these people in Canada, as it has done in Germany, in France, in Italy. It seems to me that inflation is simply a policy of ruining Peter in order to enrich Paul, and Paul is not enriched in the long run. If you raise the prices of those things which you produce, you also raise the prices of things you need. The farmer, the labourer and everyone else is in turn producer and consumer. I am afraid it will take a much bigger brain than that possessed by any hon. member of this house to work out a sound policy on those lines; and we must have longer experience in order to be sure that the results will be permanent. I pass on.
Many words have been uttered with regard to a direct reduction of our debts. This matter was before the house last evening. I was only in the chamber a very short time and I had not the privilege of following the

_____	Social Reforms-Mi. Bourassa
debate; but before coming down this afternoon I read carefully the speech delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). If one considers only the money question and the reflex action of brutal repudiation, in whole or in part, upon our credit abroad or our credit at home, the arguments propounded last evening by the Prime Minister are unanswerable. But I repeat, credit is not the only thing and the maintenance of the money power should not be our main consideration. I admit that the problem is baffling; but all efforts should be made to find a means of reducing our debts. So far as I am concerned, I think a partial repudiation, backed up by statements showing what we owe, what we earn, what our people can pay and what they cannot pay, would be more honest and less hypocritical than the so-called inflation policies which have been pursued by all governments in Europe, even by the British government when it went off the gold standard. We must prepare our creditors, both foreign and national, to accept from us, should the crisis last, a fair compensation. They will have to, in any event, in a few years. That is the only honest way in which a debtor nation can liberate itself; this should be the action taken by Canada to liberate the present and all generations to come. But if we are to present a statement of our financial situation to our creditors we must be prepared to place a levy upon the wealth of this country. This must be done to show our goodwill in meeting our creditors. Later on, when I speak of taxation, I shall have more to say of this.
As the Prime Minister said last evening, we cannot think of our indebtedness without considering the situation with which we are confronted in our railway systems. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), with whom I agree more often since he is no longer a minister of the crown, has courageously and openly suggested amalgamation. The genial and clever Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), whom curiously enough I like better since he has become a minister than I did when he was in opposition-as we say in French, he is a minister born although an Irishman-has intimated also that we must prepare for amalgamation. I am no expert; but as an old student of history I should like to express the view that it is always risky to adopt any measure of a permanent character in an effort to solve a great problem during a time of panic and crisis.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
I do not like to interrupt, but if the hon. gentleman will permit me?
Mr. BOURASSA; Certainly; I have ample time to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: I am sorry to have to correct my hon. friend but I have never intimated that we should prepare for amalgamation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Perhaps that is my French logic again; but I thought I could read that in the excellent speech which the minister delivered, I think on the second reading of Bill No. 25. But it does not matter, and I accept the minister's correction.
Instead of deciding immediately that there shall be no amalgamation or that there shall be immediate amalgamation, why not con-tine to utilize and extend, as an experiment, the provisions of the act passed last year and continued in Bill No. 25 passed at this session? I mean by this, to strengthen the control of the body created to harmonize our two systems, subject always to the supreme authority of the state. The state may be represented by this cabinet to-day, perhaps by that cabinet to-morrow or perhaps by the cabinet over here the day after.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: Never!

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
It does not matter; it
does not make much difference. Napoleon the third, who finished his reign in folly, but who was a good conspirator and, like some of my friends in the three parties, a shrewd politician, once said to one of his ministers, "Never say never in politics."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Balfour said the same
thing.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Oh yes, of course; it is obvious. It is very prudent.
I was going to say that whatever party is in power, it has not the right, in the fulfilment of its trusteeship to parliament and to the people of Canada, to abandon its supreme control over any body created by parliament for carrying out any of the powers of administration delegated by parliament to the government. But with that reservation of principle, I say that the body charged with the management of our railways should have much greater powers over what I call capital issues. It should receive-always with the same reservation-the power to suppress useless lines and to sell some of those costly hotels, ships and other works of luxury built up during our years of folly and extravagance. And, in conjunction with the state, it should devise means of reducing or contracting the debt of the two railways, both its capital stock and its debenture stock. Above all-

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
and this I suppose is on the way towards accomplishment; at least I hope so-there should be an end to foolish capital expenditures; there should be stringent economy in operation, compatible with effective service.
In the Duff report a good deal has been made of the competition to which the railways are subject, thanks to the development of the truck and autocar service. May I repeat what I have stated more than once in this parliament, in the old days as well as in more recent times? Why do our great services, why do our governments never go outside the British Empire or the United States to look for examples? On this very question of automobile competition, had they gone to France, they would have found that the great railway companies in France, and more especially the Paris-Lyon-Mediterranee -the P.L.M.-instead of waiting until competition had become disastrous, instead of bewailing the condition, and asking for special legislation to maintain their monopoly, took hold of the road traffic and put into operation the most splendid automobile service that exists in any of the countries I know of; so that an Englishman can land at Boulogne or Calais, and traverse the whole of France, stopping at any place he likes, putting up at the best hotels or in more modest places, reaching the coast of Italy by way of that beautiful country, the upper Seine valley, the Rhone valley, the Cote d'Azur, right through, by means of autocars owned and operated by that great railway system. Why did not our chiefs of railways take a short trip to France to study that system before asking the provincial governments or the federal government to take steps to do away with the competition against them?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
They were watching each
other too closely.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Just one word more with regard to railways. It has been frequently stated in this house that we are handicapped by the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway is an independent company. Well, I cannot agree with that. The Canadian Pacific Railway is a creation of parliament. It was nourished by parliament, of course at the expense of the country. I do not say, unduly. I have the greatest admiration for the pioneers of that great system; and while I do not approve of every detail connected with it, generally I quite approve of the help given to the Canadian Pacific Railway by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald. But now, where are we? Where is the company and where is the country? Without discussing the manner in which it has been administered

in the last ten or twenty years, without entering into details, I say that the Canadian Pacific Railway is now indebted to this country to a sufficient degree to force the government morally to interfere in its management; and I will say why. We have guaranteed a loan by the banks to that company of $60,000,000. The Prime Minister has said that that loan is amply covered by a block of shares deposited with the banks. In case of default, will those shares belong to the government or to the banks? If they belong to the banks, it is wrong. My experience in private life and my fairly long experience in public life has taught me that he who guarantees pays, directly or indirectly. Now, whether in order to see that the guarantee given remains good -what we call in French legal parlance " le gage du pret "-or whether in anticipation of the day when the government will have to pay this $60,000,000 or a part thereof to the banks, it is the duty of the government to keep a close hand upon the administration of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to see that its finance is managed in such a way that not only will it maintain its own credit for the benefit of its shareholders, but also for the sake of our own treasury and for the sake of the people of Canada. I will put it in a short way, one which I am sure will appeal to my good friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid):	He who pays the piper calls
the tune. I might add that if I had anything to do with the payment of this piper I would sometimes call different tunes.
This brings me to government expenses. Again I lay down the general proposition that in the circumstances through which this country is passing, a complete stop should be put to every luxury expense, if I may call it so. In this respect I am sorry to differ from the Prime Minister. When I read in the newspapers that the American Senate had, for once in a century and a half, done Canada a great service by rejecting the St. Lawrence treaty, for the first time in my life I sang within myself, Hail Columbia! I do not say, mind you, that the time will never come when that great scheme, that great plan, cannot and ought not to be carried on. But I repeat the old Latin proverb:	Est
modus in rebus. We should never forget that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: What does that mean?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: There ought to be a mode and a time in doing things.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Chaque chose a son
temps.

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Yes. I lay down the same general proposition with regard to public works generally, but that I reserve for the chapter devoted to unemployment.
I come now to ordinary administrative expenditures, and I am beginning to enter ground upon which I am afraid I shall find myself in disagreement with most of my colleagues. I believe there should be a stiff reduction in several of the public services. Take the rural mail. I state frankly before the house what I have said in my own constituency: As representing a rural constituency I have always been opposed to rural mail delivery.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: Do not say that.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
That is my opinion. I am expressing my own opinion with which my hon. friends may disagree. All I ask of them is to bear with me in patience as I have done for many days and nights when I have listened to them. I believe rural mail delivery has been of no real benefit to the farmers; it has helped to destroy rural life; connected with the postal delivery of the large departmental stores, it has helped to kill local trade, to destroy local activities, with the other consequences that I shall point out when I come to the social problems proper.
Again I am going to speak of a matter which probably will raise still more objection and protest. I refer to war pensions. In order to shelter myself, so to speak-although I am used to storm and bad weather-I shall quote two or three paragraphs of an article which appeared in a journal published in Ottawa, one never known to be a mouthpiece of rebellion or of extreme pacifism or of antipathy toward the returned soldiers. In an article published in the Ottawa Journal on October 13 last I Tead this:
In 1918, the number of thosereturned soldiers-
-receiving pensions was 25,000. Five years later, 1923, the number had grown to 63,000. To-day it is over 90,000. Where in 1918, when the war closed, the cost of pensions in the treasury-
I suppose that means "to" the treasury.
-was a little over $7,000,000, it has grown in 1933 to over $40,000,000. More than 240,000 people in Canada-soldiers and dependents of soldiers-are helped by these pensions.
Then, as a comment, the newspaper says:
Canada has passed through three years of financial crisis. With hundreds of thousands of people unemployed, and purchasing power destroyed, and the crushed taxpayer unable to meet the treasury's demand for money to meet
calls for debt and relief, the situation has been a desperately difficult one. Yet through these three years, notwithstanding a fierce need for retrenchment, the country has gone on paying war pensions, has added steadily and heavily to the pensions roll.
This is something which veterans, fair minded and responsible, should surely bear in mind. They must realize something of the country's position; of its declining revenues; of the obligations it has had to face; of the calls that have been made upon it and upon the country's financial resources.
I shall not insist any more upon that point to-day.
Now, over and above war pensions, we have a frightful increase in the payment of doles to the unemployed, with a threat of a permanent financial burden, placed upon the country, on account of an unemployment which will last until we adopt stringent measures to reestablish the balance between city dwellers and rural population. What is the result? First, as regards finance applied to social needs, the war pensions and the dole system are, and will remain for years to come, an insurmountable obstacle to the adoption of a set plan of social insurance for the benefit of all classes in Canada. Without reopening old sores, without discussing whether we were right in participating in the war, in enlisting, first voluntarily, then under pressure, and thirdly by conscription, the youth of Canada to go and wage a war foreign to America, may I put this question to any fairminded man in the house? Not only to my pacifist friends, but equally to the brave men who have shown their sincerity in going to war on their own account and have not contented themselves with preaching war to others and remaining at home to enrich themselves, as so many warmongers and patriots did from 1914 to 1918, I put this question:	Is it really a
moral obligation on the part of Canada to maintain a body of men with their wives and children, men who were induced to fight for four years out of Canada, to destroy life and property, in a just war if you like-I am not discussing that? If it is, what do hon. members think of our moral obligation to thousands of good men and women who have worked all their life in Canada, for Canada, to give children to Canada and money to the exchequer of Canada? Are we going to make them lose, after fifty years of hard life, all that they have saved, and then die in misery, in order, first, to pay our creditors 100 cents on the dollar, and, second, to keep up two privileged classes, the war pensioners and the dole receivers?
So far as ordinary government expenditure is concerned, I have only one word to say.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: I do not intend to.

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
I have now to deal with a still more disagreeable subject, that is taxation. But we have to face it. We do not want to repudiate our debts-I accept the word of the Prime Minister. We have not yet found a means of restricting them. There remain only two things-curtailment, stringent curtailment of expenditure, and increase of taxation.
In that connection I want to point out
the reasons for a capital levy. At first sight

such a proposal is distasteful; all taxation is distasteful. Unfortunately this suggestion has been presented, not only in Canada but in most countries, by socialists, by would-be revolutionists, under the name of conscription of wealth. I might ask, as has been asked frequently: If it was right to conscript men to destroy, is it wrong to conscript wealth to reconstruct? But I will leave that aside. If the men of wealth, if the great corporations of this country understood the situation as it is, there would be no need to conscript wealth; they would themselves enlist freely, voluntarily, and help in reducing the debt. For my part may I say that after forty years of assiduous labour I have been able to put aside, out of the money I earned from year to year, about $25,000. I suppose my friends to the left will not consider me as a wicked capitalist. I had a little inheritance which, as I felt in duty bound to do, I have transmitted intact to my children. What I received from my parents I reserved for my children; and as soon as they come of age I give them their share according to what I consider their merits. The other is what I have saved. Now I tell you quite frankly that I would be mighty glad to give, out of that $25,000, $1,000 to the government to help reduce the debt. But it should be on three conditions: first, that every Canadian should pay his share in the same proportion ; second, that the whole of that contribution should go to the reduction of debt; and third, that by courageous measures of economy and taxation, budgets should be balanced hereafter. By doing so I would consider my $1,000 well placed.
The difficulty is that big business men, with their genius and perhaps also their greed, will not pay their share voluntarily; but I think the time has come for governments, starting with the federal government, to educate public opinion, and particularly the opinion of those who possess, that such a form of taxation, far from being a measure of confiscation, would be the safest measure of conservation. Once they have been taxed in order to alleviate the burden of public debts, once the economic situation generally has been bettered by such a diminution of debt, then their affairs will grow, and what they keep of their wealth will be better preserved by having paid some of it to maintain or rather to restore the finances of the country, than by trying to enjoy it unduly until the crash comes.
But there is more than that, sir. Of course I admit that I am an old-timer and have queer ideas. At * times I seem to be the representative duly appointed, morally speak-

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
ing, of all the cranks in Canada from Sydney to Prince Rupert; from some of the letters I receive I think I can claim that title fairly. But I also receive communications from people of fair minds and right thought belonging to all parties. The thought which I am going to express is that which I think is in the minds, and even more in the heart and conscience, of a large number of Canadians. This generation, to which we belong, responsible as it is-not all the individuals but the whole community under the law of solidarity-this generation which is responsible for the follies which preceded the war, railway follies and others, which is responsible for the follies of the war, which is responsible for the perhaps greater follies which followed the war, has not the right to leave to the next generation, to your children and mine, the full burden of the payment for our follies. What would you think of a prodigal father who, having piled up debt after debt in debauchery and extravagance, would say to his creditors: My children will pay you? That would be worse than the cruelty described by Christ as being almost impossible: "Or what man is there of you, whom if his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?" That is what we are doing.
I am now coming near to the day when I will have to render account to my God for what I have done in private and public life, and I do not want to leave this world without having protested against the injustice that will be perpetrated if we leave future generations to pay the whole of the debts that have been piled up thanks to our lack of foresight, to say no more.
Now, coming to ordinary taxation-I am sorry that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is not here but perhaps his attention will be called to just one instance I am going to give.
I am in favour of maintaining and perhaps of increasing, with care, the income tax. But I point out here publicly that which I have shown to various ministers who have succeeded to office, either in the treasury or in the Department of National Revenue, since I came back to parliament. Since last year, taxation is imposed on government annuities over SI,200 and on ordinary revenues over $1,000. I must say that owing to a judgment rendered in 1858 by a good English judge who had more knowledge of law than of economics, or even of simple mathematics, an annuity is considered as being total income, which is of course absurd and nonsensical. Then, in our devotion to everything British, a judge-I was going to say an equally stupid
judge, but I shall not say that-a judge in Canada copied the judgment delivered in England, and gave the same decision.
I do not wish to carry the argument to greater length, but shall simply give some figures. Suppose a man of sixty years decided to invest a sum of $25,000 in government bonds. Under the last issue he could get $25,000 worth of bonds for $23,362.50. In twenty years time-and I am referring to a twenty-year issue-he would receive $20,000 in interest. That is, he would receive interest for twenty years at the rate of $1,000 a year, and would not pay a single cent of income tax. Suppose another man, the same age, had taken an equal sum of $23,362.50 and purchased from the same government a life annuity. He would receive annually $2,247.47. Of course, everybody knows that that includes a revenue of only four per cent on the S23,362.50. The rest is capital reduction. He would receive in interest, during these twenty years, $18,690. But during that same period, under the present rate, he would pay $638 of income tax. Is that just? That is a capital levy. I have just said that I have no objection to a capital levy, but let it be a levy on all capital. Why pick out a class of people who have been invited to purchase annuities? I have before me circidars sent by government agents inviting such purchases. Of course those purchases are very advantageous to the government, because the capital is never totally paid back. It is paid by instalments, according to tables of mortality which are very well calculated. This procedure is much more advantageous to the state than would be the selling of bonds. Nevertheless, you let go scot free the man who purchases a bond, and who will receive your interest of four and a half per cent; and then you tax a man who is only drawing an annuity. If he dies within twenty years you inherit the portion of his capital he has not received, and besides, you have collected taxation. That shows how all matters of taxation have to be scrutinized, and I believe this statement applies to almost every form of it.

He can get only $1,200.

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
Yes, now. And this also is a mistaken policy, because if there is one form of investment which any government should invite, it would be those annuities. But at the request, or rather, under pressure from the life insurance companies, the government limited the amount. They have thereby lost millions of dollars upon which they would have paid only four per cent, while they have launched debentures giving four and a half per cent, plus commissions to brokers.
I am not going to dwell longer with the subject of taxation, because there may be an opportunity in the debate on the budget. I shall not mention the sales tax, excise taxes and so on, but shall simply lay down three principles which I hope the government, and the Minister of Finance in particular, will consider.
First, if we want to have some degree of financial balance and social justice, there must be an understanding between federal and provincial authorities, including of course municipal authorities, as to the manner or the mode in which they levy taxation upon the various communities in this country. In some provinces we have double income tax, while in others there is biut one. A consideration of this matter should be the main object of the next conference between federal and provincial authorities.
Second, in every form of taxation, either direct or indirect, I urge upon the government the necessity of caring for the small trader, the small industrialist, the small proprietor, even the small capitalist or what they call in France "l'epargniste" or even "le rentier." I know that at times those people are called social parasites. I suppose in Europe, where estates have been transmitted from generation to generation in certain families, some might be called social parasites, unless they render to the state and to the nation some other services. But in this country those parasites do not exist. Practically all of those small proprietors living on their revenues in their old age, are retired workers or retired employees. For years and years they have been meritorious contributors to the general welfare of the community, municipal, provincial and federal. So far they have been the best supporters of moral and social order, the cement of the social structure. They are by

nature, by instinct and by interest, essentially conservative, in the best sense of the word. But if ruined by taxation or otherwise they may become the most desperate revolutionists, because there can be no hope for them in beginning a new life. If hon. members have followed, as I have, the trend of events in Europe since the war, they must know that it is this class, this small middle class, ruined and oppressed, which on the one hand has supplied the forces of communism and on the other hand the counter forces of fascism. Do we want that in Canada? We want neither the one nor the other. My friends to the left do not want it any more than the Liberals or the Conservatives, but that is what we are preparing.
Finally, in all matters of taxation, remember first, last and above all the rights of the family. Here and there we hear of the necessity of having a larger population to help us in paying our debts and lifting the burden of taxation. Agreed. But vhat do we want? Do we want more foreigners to come in, or shall we give the preference to the children of Canadian families? By Canadian families I mean good Canadian citizens of whatever race they may be, whether born in Canada or outside. But of that more towards the dose of my remarks.
Before I leave the question of social and economic reform I want to say a word about the life insurance companies. The Prime Minister referred to them last night, and quite rightly so. In a sense the life insurance companies, from the social viewpoint, are more important than the banks. In a new country, and more especially in the United States and Canada, the life insurance companies have become the financial mainstay of the family. Quite a number of individuals belonging to the professions, to trade or industry, and who have allowed themselves and their families to live what I call an extravagant life, have nevertheless devoted a large portion of what they earned to purchasing insurance policies. Take, again, the small tradesman or the farmer who puts aside a few dollars each year to purchase a policy of $1,000 for his widow and family. All that money goes into the coffers of insurance companies. We often hear about the trusteeship of the banks with regard to the funds entrusted to them; but the amount of private funds in the hands of the banks, as was so ably demonstrated by the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) in a speech delivered in Toronto a few days before the opening of the session, and which by the way was one of the best I ever read from him or anyone else, is only four per cent of the so-

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
called money or of the apparent volume of the transactions which the banks carry on between debtors and creditors of the banks. That is what a bank plays with. On the other hand, the funds in the hands of insurance companies are composed of real money entrusted to the company by policyholders, and most of it for the benefit of their families. Is it not the primary duty of the state to see that that money is properly invested and kept as safe as it possibly can be? But how has that duty been done? I know that we are now face to face with the decision of the privy council, that the control of insurance companies rests with the provincial governments; but surely this question ought to be dealt with, first by conference, and then by concurrent legislation, so that, whatever governmental authority is exercised over insurance companies, the funds entrusted to their hands and upon which the bread and lives of so many hundreds of thousands of Canadians depend will be kept safe. Is that done at the present time?
I want to avoid as much as possible personal issues, and I do not want to be unduly harsh upon the directors of the large companies, but after all we are here to say the truth-at least we ought to be here for that.
Take the case of the Sun Life Assurance Company, by far the largest concern in Canada. I have taken these figures from its last report, dated December 31. 1932. Their total assets amount to 8611,436,152.70. Of that amount real estate represents $26,546,571.26; and in this last figure is included the cost price of that tower of Babel in Montreal, the head office of the company, amounting to $21,392,282.36. It is quite illustrative of the follies of the last ten years. That tower of Babel stands beside that immense hole, empty of earth and of everything else, which is the future Canadian National Railway station in Montreal-an abyss on the one hand, a pyramid of extravagance on the other. How many millions would that tower fetch at prices prevailing to-day?
Take the item of bonds, debentures, and debenture stocks. In the books of the company they are carried at $117,393,222.98; but that has been scaled down by the superintendent of insurance here to $107,861,810.99, a reduction of about ten million dollars.
Take the item of stocks. Preferred stocks are carried on the books of the company at $23,244,147.07, and that has been scaled down to $19,576,944.04. Common stocks are carried at S298,954,632.81, and that figure has been brought down to $292,472,334.11. Other assets, $164,978,492.30.
In other words that so-called trust fund of the Sun Life Assurance Company is composed, up to 48 per cent, of the common stocks of all sorts of concerns in America, north and south. Those great believers in the national creed of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) are great believers in the Canadian people following that creed; but they do not believe in it so far as the company itself is concerned, because they invest all the money they can outside of Canada.
The liabilities of the company are shown as $603,438,205.87, of which 8586,007,260.37 is due to policyholders, most of it due to women and children in Canada. Other liabilities are shown as $17,430,945.50. So, to guarantee this $586,007,260.37 due to the policy-holders there is a surplus altogether of $5,997,946.89, exclusive of the capital stock, $2,000,000.
Now what are all those stocks worth? Nobody knows. Without betraying any confidence I might say that four or five years ago, when that company came before parliament to secure the right of issuing more capital shares, I had given some study to the situation of insurance companies, especially the Sun Life, and I went to see one of the most authoritative men in this country on this subject. I said to him, "On the face of their report are they not bankrupt?"-That was the year they raised the dividend to their shareholders from 50 to 75 per cent. He replied, "Of course, but what is the use of saying it? It would create a panic."
Without insisting too much, I might say that some years previously, when the Canadian Northern Company came before this parliament for assistance, and when the present Prime Minister fought against it, what was the reason given in and out of parliament for giving that assistance ? It was said: If we do not rescue the Canadian Northern and Mackenzie and Mann at the expense of the country, it means the bankruptcy of the Bank of Commerce and the Canada Life Insurance Company.
Now I ask, is it fair that the public should be blackmailed and the public treasury tapped because the powers that be, federal or provincial, have not exercised beforehand their duty and found out what was the real situation in these great companies before they came to ask for assistance?
I could give three or four more examples, but it would take too long. It all amounts to this: If a small trader or industrialist, a small banker or capitalist, operates for some time at the expense of the public and goes to the wall, he is put in bankruptcy; and if he has been crooked he is put in jail. But if you

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
steal millions you are safe, because if you are denounced it will shake the confidence of the public. I should like to relate a story, one which I think is true, to show how such things react in various countries, but I shall resist the temptation of giving names. Not long ago, a meeting of shareholders or debenture holders of one of those large concerns, organized by one of our largest banks and supported, operated and mal-administered by several of our kings and captains of finance, was held in Montreal. A Scotchman was present, representing the creditors of Great Britain. He asked if Mr. So-and-So was there, and he was told he was. He said, "I want to tell you that man is the greatest scoundrel in Canada." "Oh, no, pardon me; Sir So-and-So is a greater scoundrel than the other." That is the impression left upon our foreign creditors by some of our great financial operations. Such a thing may endanger the credit of Canada just as much as the bringing to account of these perpetrators of frauds and exploitations. At least, that is my old way of looking at things.
This brings me to another matter, the control of stock exchanges. I brought this matter up, I think thirty-one years ago, in the old parliament. I do not mean to boast, but I have had no personal experience with these organizations. I would not go to a stockbroker's office or to a stock exchange any more than I would go to a house of prostitution. I do not like them. To me, stock gambling is to legitimate financial operations what prostitution is to marriage. I am not referring to the regular sale and purchase of stocks and debentures, but this is, anly a small percentage of the business carried on by these organizations. The legitimate purchase and sale of securities is, I am told, not more than one per cent of the total business transacted. Most of it is gambling, playing on ups and downs. It might be said, so much the worse for those who lose. If they were the only ones concerned, then I would agree. It is a different thing when a man goes to a gambling house and loses money at cards, or bets on the wrong horse at a race track. Stock gambling brought about the crash of 1929. It means the shaking of the financial structure of the country; it means damage to the credit of corporations, honestly administered; it means damage to the credit of the country; it means damage to the economic life of the whole nation. It is the duty of the government to stop this. When I brought up this matter before,
I think in the session of 1903, I received all sorts of compliments from people on all sides. I received letters from people in Montreal,

Toronto and elsewhere, stating that at last the truth was out and hoping that the government would act. Of course, the Liberal government of that day did not act; the Conservative government which followed did not act, nor did any other government. Why? Do hon. members know what people are saying? They say: You will never get reform in that way because too many members of parliament are interested in the game. I do not believe that, but that is the impression abroad.
I was told last week by one of the safest, one of the keenest bankers in Canada, one who enjoys the confidence of the whole financial and commercial public, the confidence of all parties and all governments, that three years ago all the stock exchange brokers in Montreal, with the exception of perhaps two or three, were absolutely bankrupt. They had to be carried by the banks because the banks were afraid of the reactions which might follow. Are we going to allow such things to continue? I have reminded the house already of a very remarkable reform brought about in Italy, not by Mussolini, but by the Liberal government of Giolitti, the safest man who has been at the head of affairs of that country during the last half century. He was frightened at the speculative spirit that had developed in his country. The Germans were coming in and investing millions, and Italians with their instinctive gambling spirit-they have had their mora and their lotteries for centuries-began playing with hundreds of thousands of lire. This gambling was injuring the credit of the country; and many families were ruined. Giolitti decided that there must be a stop. He put through a very simple law which rendered null and void the sale' or purchase of any bond or share unless it was paid for one hundred per cent and registered in the name of the purchaser. Of course there were protests:	Restriction of trade! Encroachment upon individual liberty! But he let them cry. Later on, he was told by practically two-thirds of the business men of Italy, some of whom had criticized him most severely, that he had saved Italy. I repeat, why should not we go outside the countries under the British flag or under the star spangled banner for guidance in some matters? Intelligence, especially economic intelligence, is to be found elsewhere. Take France, for instance. I have friends in the various parties in that country. I do not like their politics, either national or international. However, economically speaking, France has the best record of any occidental country in the world.

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
Vi hy this is so I shall reserve for a future occasion; but at this time I would remind the house that in that country, the government has preserved a fairly equal balance between utter neglect of its duties and undue interference. I think the time has come for us to act in a similar manner.
I shall not refer to the control of prices, an extremely important matter, as this is the subject matter of the study of a committee of this house. I shall not do more than say to the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Des-lauriers) that I concur entirely with the views he expressed some time ago in connection with the fuel situation in Montreal. Do hon. members realize the social and moral danger arising from such a situation? As we say in French:	Put yourself in the shoes of the
average individual in Montreal. I suppose there are in Montreal at the present time some three or four hundred thousand people either poverty stricken or on the verge of poverty. Just imagine these people having to pay three; times what they should pay for their coal during a winter like this. An inquiry was started, but imagine their feelings when they read that after Senator Webster had given his testimony he started on a cruise around the world in one of our palatial boats. No doubt when he was going through the strait of Gibraltar and was contemplating that magnificent rock, no doubt when he was nearing the Red sea, and glanced at the pyramids and perhaps put a question to the sphinx; no doubt when he reached the Straits Settlements, having been in contact with all races and nations of the world, he forgot all about the coal situation in Montreal. But I ask again, what are the feelings of the people who had to pay four times as much for the coal as it was worth-the coal controlled by the monopoly organized by Senator Webster? Do you think they have much regard for our leading classes, for the Senate of which that hon. gentleman is an ornament, or the House of Commons which is supposed to stand in defence of the rights of poor people, or the governments-because this refers to Quebec as well as Ottawa-which are supposed to care so much for the masses during an election? Of course, we all love the people when an election comes on; we are prepared to give them everything they want. But after the election is over, we allow them to be fleeced by our friends, party contributors and pillars of church and state and social order.
I pass now to control of credit, which is perhaps the most important question. I will not speak of rural credit, but I would invite those who take an interest in this subject to study how an Italian Jew, Luzzatti, solved
the problem in Italy before he became Minister of Finance, in the same cabinet with Giolitti. He started, in characteristic Italian fashion, in a very small way, organizing a few individuals in this village, in that part of the country, and elsewhere, and so on, until, within a few years, not only did the small rural banks save agriculture, the culture of vines, but when Italy was on the verge of bankruptcy, thanks to the megalomania of Crispi, who launched Italy into the arms of the triple alliance, it was these small banks that saved Italy. The big banks had invested so much money in armaments, in big industries and other large concerns that they had no more money to lend the government. It was the farmers, the vine growers of Italy, through their banks, who saved the situation and put Italy once more on the safe path.
Here and now I predict that if the countries of Europe, Italy especially, are spared war or revolution within the next ten years, they will pass through this crisis much more quickly than we shall and will emerge in a far better condition, because they have not lost their senses to the extent that we have; they have not abused credit as much as we have, both for public and private enterprises.
I will not refer to our banks except to state quite candidly that my attitude towards these institutions, in matters of credit, is the opposite of the general attitude in Canada. My reproach to the banks is not that they have refused credit but that they have given it too freely in times of extravagance. It is all very well to say that the banks do not lend money on land, on mines or on stocks; but when money was abundant, when business was supposed to be prosperous-business as a matter of fact was ill; it was suffering from a fever of folly in the years which preceded the crash,-any ten individuals in Montreal could borrow money on notes signed by one another-what for? To put into trade? No, sir; to speculate, to gamble in lands and mines and stocks. They did it either directly or through their stockholders. It would be interesting to know the amount of credit which was once given to one single stockbroking agency in Montreal-why not name it?-Holt, Gundy & Co., by the Royal Bank, the head of which is Sir Herbert Holt, associated with the same Holt, Gundy. It would be interesting to find that out.
Now there is another form of credit in which I take a good deal of interest, from the point of view of the family, of small people, and that is the sale of goods on terms or on instalments. That has done a good deal to ruin small trade; it has ruined families, not only financially but morally.



Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
Dishonesty in business has increased in the city of Montreal during the last ten years to astounding proportions, and that owing largely to the system of sales on instalments, protected as it is by a law passed some years ago in Quebec.

speechtext: Does that apply only to Montreal?

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
No, but Montreal is a
large city. There are many people whose dwellings are filled with goods unpaid for, over which the landlord has no claim and which the legal owners, the original sellers, do not care to take back inasmuch as they have received very often enough money on such goods. They leave them there with the result that the tenant who has purchased the goods is in debt, does not pay his rent, and the landlord suffers, the city suffers and everyone suffers. In the long run the seller himself suffers because he has too much out on credit.
We should put a stop to this as well as to the growth of the system of coupons and premiums and "drawing cards." I was amazed at a memorandum given me last fall by one of the most important tobacco firms in Montreal, showing the amount of money which they are forced to disburse in order to cope with the competition of other firms who resort to this sort of thing. That is not only an imposition on competing firms and factories, but it is also unfair to the trade; because the so-called premiums which they give fill up certain stores with goods purchased at much less than cost price and therefore sold in unfair competition against the ordinary trader.
Now to sum up this chapter, I say that the main concern of parliament and of the government should be to revive local life, to revive local trade half ruined by the large departmental stores, aided by the state through postal distribution and rural mail delivery. We should do all we can to revive local industry and husbandry, destroyed by trusts and combines protected by tariffs and defective companies acts, both federal and provincial. Village life is undermined, rural communities are depleted, cities and towns are congested, with all the economic, political and social consequences that follow, a far greater menace than bolshevism in Russia, because that is the hotbed of bolshevism in Canada.
My friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), on a subject akin to this, said, "Oh, but we cannot turn back the hands of the clock." I beg to differ from him on that. It all depends on the clock. I have known clocks, well made, the hands of which could be turned backwards or forwards. I

will not say the same for cheap clocks-and our economics, though they have cost us much money, are cheap in quality. But surely if the clock runs amuck it can be stopped; the pendulum can be adjusted, the wheels cleaned and set in order so that the clock will keep correct time and mark the right hour all day long. Is that not the real thing we should have in view? I contend that it is. I contend that what we need, from government down to the poorest individual in the land, is a return to normal life. What we need is to bring back, not only to the farm, as has been mentioned frequently in the house, but to the village as well, a large number of people who have been lured, by the war and by the false industries started during the war, to the large cities.
May I recommend to the attention of all the marvellous work done in a modest way by a modest employee of the Canadian National Railways in Montreal, Mr. J. E. Laforce? Not only by lectures over the radio, but also by his own active work, he brings to the Abitibi and various other districts, once or twice a month, sometimes ten, sometimes twenty families whom he places where it is most likely they will succeed. He does not organize things in a spectacular way, with big trains filled up with men, women and children who are thrown into the desert, the forest or the marsh without any prospect of success. No; he knows the place; he knows the people; he knows their needs; and what money he gets from governments he knows will not be misplaced. If those humble efforts of a single modest French Canadian employee had been, I shall not say helped, because he has been helped sufficiently, but followed up; if his example were followed now and repeated in every large centre of Canada, that would be a far greater contribution to social readjustment than many great schemes.
We must also look to a reduction in the cost of living and labour. Here again I am afraid that I shall not be in accord with most people. The general opinion seems to be that we should keep everything up. I say that we should bring everything down-not down into the abyss, but down to the level on which most human beings were accustomed to live prior to the war, where we shall find rest, not in the clouds, not on the tops of mountains, not in the depth of abysses and marshes, but on good solid level ground.
We must also encourage thrift and honest production. Some years ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce launched a creed urging all consumers in Canada to purchase Canadian made goods. An appeal should be made to all producers in Canada, from manufac-

Social Rejorms-Mr. Bourassa
turers down to labourers and farmers, to give us honest products. Since the war, the quality of many of our products has deteriorated owing to lack of conscience on the part not only of managers but of labourers as well. The main concern of most people, to-day, among those at the head of affairs, is to make as much money as possible, and of those at the foot to get rid of their work with the least possible effort of intelligence and of the hand. A sense of duty is lacking in all classes.
It is said: But you will thereby lower the standard of living. Here again I am afraid that I shall find myself more in isolation than ever. What is meant by a high standard of living? Of course, if cost is meant, I admit that more money is spent by the average Canadian or American than by the average European. But if by standard of living is meant a certain balance in human activities, a certain degree of satisfaction to the mind and to the heart, and comfort to the body, I have no hesitation in saying this:	I have travelled
and lived in eight or ten countries in Europe. From the view point of either moral, intellectual, artistic or even material life, the standard of life of the French, the Italian, the Swiss, the Belgian, the Dutch, the German, not to speak of the Britisher, is higher than that of Canadians and Americans. One of the closest students of things British, a great admirer of Great Britain and the British mind, a Frenchman who knows all parts of the British Empire and, by the way, a Protestant by religion, Mr. Andre Siegfried, whom I knew thirty-five years ago, who is still a close student of all matters pertaining to England and her empire, and to the United States i epublic as well, published three or four years ago, at the inception of this crisis, a most illuminating book on the situation in England. He then predicted, with evidence at the back of his opinion, that England would never recover her supremacy in matters of trade and industry until her people renounced their false ideas with regard to standard of life, because the continental European, more modest, more economical and at the same time more concerned about giving a little time of his life to thought, study and art, contenting himself with more modest foods and humbler garments, but at the same time having more satisfaction in life, gave better work than did the Englishman. If we had to compare continental Europe with America, I am afraid the comparison would be still more disastrous.
That brings me to the question of unemployment. I shall be very brief on this question because it has been so frequently dis-74726-105A
cussed. I immediately express the view that we must as soon as possible suppress the dole and also the concentration camps. Let us give work, yes, but here I want to say what I think about work. Give big works, spectacular work? No. That again shows the spirit of the parvenu. Trans^Canadian highways, big buildings? No. That means that half the money goes to contractors and in payment of machinery. Further, it means simply the transportation of thousands of men from one part of the country to another, thereby training in a wandering and homeless life hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I say, on the contrary, that we should have numerous small works, useful works, everywhere. As regards the constituency that I represent, I pointed out to the permanent official who had to deal with relief funds, that this government alone had spent in my constituency some $6,000 or $7,000 that could have been spared because they were spent on useless work. Of course he said that that was due, and I suppose rightly so, to the fact that the expenditure had been approved by the Quebec government. I said: "When you give money to Quebec, surely you should know what is done with it." It is useless building public halls, roads to enable club men m Montreal to go more comfortably at the time of trout fishing or deer hunting from that city to the midst of my constituency. Build useful works, works that will result in peimanent benefit to the people of the locality, scattering men here and there, in villages' so that they cannot be a threat to any place where they are and still less a threat to the community. In other words, a great problem in this respect is what some people might call conscription of labour. Call it that if you like. As I said about conscription of wealth, labour having been conscripted to kill and destroy, surely it is as legitimate to conscript labour to reconstruct and give life. But it is not necessary to call it by that odious name. The problem is, a better distribution of work and labour with a view to reestablishing a balance between rural and in ban population and sending back some of the blood now concentrated in the centres through the arteries to all parts of the country.
That brings me to a much discussed question, that of the maintenance of public order. Here again I am sorry but I cannot quite agree with my hon. friends to the left. The main function of the state is to maintain public order for the benefit of all.
