Who said it was not?

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa

maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext:
But the state cannot
exercise that power with moral authority unless the repression of disorder takes place everywhere, from top to bottom. Torture has been reestablished in Canada, to secure avowals from people not even declared guilty by courts of law. Scourging is now being inflicted on burglars; perhaps it is necessary, but my sense of justice and that of many other Canadians is not satisfied. If we are going to reestablish forms of punishment which were discarded two hundred years ago as barbarous, and inflict them on the small criminal, then I suggest that the pillory should be reestablished in the Place d'Armes in Montreal, and men responsible for the present economic and social unrest be put in the stocks, so that the good people from town and country will have the right to go and throw cabbages at them, as was done in London and Paris and elsewhere, when there was some kind of social justice. I would not kill them, but I would give them a good
lesson.	.
Something must be done to alleviate the " hard, cruel, relentless " burden now weighing upon the shoulders of the masses. I borrow those words from the encyclical of Pope Pius XI. Men of wealth who abuse their power, keeping the poor, keeping us all, in various degrees, in subjection, must be brought to their senses or severely punished. This is not revolution. Co back in history. I will give only two instances. Find out in what manner Louis XIV dealt with Fouquet, in what manner Napoleon dealt with Ouvrard; and you will see how, under monarchical government in one case, dictatorial in the second, but with the consent of the people, _ millionaire financiers who had abused their power were dealt with under the law.
But having said so much, I also say it is the duty of the government to suppress, and better still to prevent riots; not so much punishing the rioters, most of whom are poor, misguided fools, but by punishing, first, those who, by their injustice to the poor and the oppressed, cause such a state of suffering that they lose their head and follow the first demagogue who appeals to them. Secondly, I go further than the Minister of Justice went last year; rather than punishing the rioter when the riot has taken place, I say boldly: Gag the demagogue.
I know my hon. friend near me is concerned about liberty of speech, and I know he is sincere. Before I answer him on this point, however, I give for a second time a friendly warning to my Quebec friends, right or left: cease charging the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with com-

munistic views. You know it is untrue, you know it is a slander, you know it is unfair to a man with whose ideas you may differ, but whose sincerity no one can question. I repeat, a day may come, and come sooner than you think, when people who now denounce the leader of the C.C.F. will regard him as a bulwark against demagogy and communism. Eveiyone who reads what is taking place knows that he has no bitterer enemies in Canada than the communists, he has been denounced by them from the beginning. But I repeat, I cannot share his view that liberty of speech must be untrammelled. Liberty of speech, like every other kind of liberty, ceases to be legitimate when it endangers social order and interferes with the liberty of others.
Much has been said about those trials for blasphemy in Quebec. Some have said it is a return to mediaevalism. May I repeat what I stated during the debate on the address? Try to understand the feelings of all. For forty years I have endeavoured to understand the viewpoint of the westerner, for example, and on many occasions I have been able to make my fellow citizens in Quebec understand some of the problems of the west. Likewise, try to understand us. Realize this, I say it from the bottom of my heart, that an insult to our God, an insult to our church, is more hurtful to our sense of human dignity than an insult to father or mother. Shall we then, those of us who have authority, let the first demagogue on the street^ throw mud at the name we revere and at the institution in which we were born and in which we wish to die? Is it not interfering with the liberty of those poor bleeding people who have no other consolation but in praying to God in remaining from birth to death in the arms of their church, to have it insulted without any protection being given to them? We do not ask anybody to believe as we believe, but we ask not to be insulted. As I said to one of those demagogues: How much bread will it give to the poor, or what good will it do them, that you throw mud at the name of God, or throw insults at men and women who, for forty or fifty years, have lived a life of sacrifice to feed the poor, clean the unclean, give some kind of moral life where there was only dirt, corruption and degradation? Respect us as we respect others.
But, it is said, we must save democracy. I must confess that to me democracy is very much a catch word. During the war I was once bold enough to state before an audience in the United States something, that the moment I said it, I thought would bring thunder on my head. You remember Presi-

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
dent Wilson's famous saying, "We fight to make the world safe for democracy." After I had seen the turn of things, the passions, the greed, the ambitions of all nations as revealed in the peace negotiations, I said to that audience: Ladies and gentlemen, I am afraid we must slightly correct President Wilson's saying, and admit that we have fought to make the world safe for hypocrisy. The famous definition: " Government of the people, for the people and by the people," is at once a truth and a falsity. "Of the people" -of course, it is obvious; every government is a government of the people. " For the people"-that is what it ought to be, but unfortunately very few governments are for the people governed. They are first for the people who exercise government. "By the people"-that has never been and will never be. Under a democracy the people, once in a while, delegate to certain legislative or governing bodies individuals who are supposed to represent their views. But which of us can claim that upon any question coming before the house, he is voicing the views or the aspirations of the people he represents? Of course not.
Socialism is sounder-I am not afraid to say this-than either democracy or liberalism. As a reaction against individualism, it has been a godsend to the world; but in practice it is evincing itself as a mere entrance either to communism or to fascism, two forms of tyranny.
It may be asked: Why not stick to the good old conservatism? Well, at the risk of appearing very critical, I say that conservatism is an impossibility. In its strict sense and usual practice, it means the conservation of everything which exists-of the bad as well as of the good. It means the conservation of the bad germs which bring about revolution. If you wish to preserve or restore what is good in society, you must boldly destroy what is wrong.
On one point, however, there must be agreement. Whether we like it or not, a new social order has to arise. May I make a slight correction and suggest that what we need is not a new social order but a restoration of the old one, a reconstruction, which would mean making use of all that was true, good, enduring and fruitful in the old society, and giving a new construction adaptable to present needs. Under such a restored order there ought to be a just balance between authority and liberty, between individual right and social duty.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, may I crave the indulgence of the house, for the remainder of this speech which is already too long, to resort to my notes? It is the first, and probably the last time in thirty-eight years, I have done so. However, as these are very delicate subjects, I have preferred to put down in writing what I have to say.
Under the law of nature spiritualized by Christianity, social order rests on three bases, of unequal importance:	property, family,
religion; the material, the social, the spiritual.
Property is theft, said Proud'hon-" La propriety c'est le vol." That proposition raised a cry of horror and reprobation, especially from the ranks of property owners. But the greatest Catholic social leader of Germany, I might say of Europe, Ketteler, Bishop of Mayence-he whom Pope Leo XIII since called his " predecessor " in the work of social reform-Ketteler had the courage to acknowledge that Proud'hon's paradox " contains both a huge lie and a fertile truth." Of course I am quoting the translation. " We must first destroy what is true therein to make it a complete falsehood

It is the false right of property which gave birth to the false theory of communism." That is, the false right of Droperty under modem legislation. In other words, the right of property is real; but in the concrete, much property is acquired by theft and held unjustly, with the complicity of man-made laws.
According to Catholic teaching, from Christ to Pius XI, through Paul, Thomas Aquinas, Bossuet, and thousands of others, no man has an absolute right of property on any thing. God is the creator and sole owner of all earthly goods. In his munificence he puts at the disposal of mankind, of all men, women and children, for their sustenance, all that the earth contains and produces. No individual has the right to possess himself of anything to the detriment of his fellow beings. All that any individual can claim is the right to enjoy the fruits of his labour, to capitalize them-I do not like that word; I would rather say to stabilize-and freely dispose of them, by testament or otherwise, but never to the detriment of other individuals and of the community at large. Whenever any individual, or group of individuals, violates that law of social justice and order, it is the right, nay, the pre-eminent duty of the state, representing the community, and bound to protect the poor, the oppressed-as the kings of France, when Christianity prevailed over Roman law, swore to, in their coronation oath-it is the duty of the state to intervene and check greed, accumulation of wealth, combines, and all the devices by which the

Social Reforms-Mr. Bourassa
kings of finance oppress the poor and deprive them of their natural right to acquire their modest share of temporal goods.
Property, private or corporate, to be legitimate, must be honestly acquired, properly administered and used for righteous purposes. To be useful to society it ought to be fairly distributed amongst the largest possible number of individuals in the community.
Now-and on this point I call the special attention of my French speaking and Catholic colleagues on both sides of the house-this form of property, the small property, the most legitimate, the most useful to society, is being destroyed in Canada, in Quebec, in the city of Montreal especially, by capitalism, by taxation, by false economics and a foolish standard of life, as rapidly and effectively as in Russia by communism and bolshevistic rule or misrule.
The situation is still graver when you relate property to family. According to Pope Leo XIII, the right of man to private property- limited as aforesaid-is strengthened by the "extension" of man into the "domestic society," the family.
Family is the essential cell of society. To Canadians, this obvious truth need not be demonstrated, although it would be easy to point out the disintegrating influence exercised on the family, in Quebec, by French jacobinism as expressed in our Quebec civil jode, and all through Canada by the no less destructive individualism transfused to us by the Manchester school of thought.
All I wish to say now, as a warning to our leaders, in church and state, is this:	Family,
like private property, is at present being threatened, nay, demoralized and destroyed, in Canada, in Quebec, in the city of Montreal more perhaps than anywhere else, by capitalism, materialism, taxation and extravagance, as surely, if less ruthlessly, as in Russia, under the yoke Of Lenin and his disciples. In Montreal and other large centres, it is almost impossible to-day, for thousands of good, honest men and women, to maintain a home and a family, and for thousands of young folks to found one. Hence a rapid spread of anti-conceptional practices among married people, a frightful increase of immorality in the young people of both sexes, a marked degradation of faith and morals among all. I am referring now to Catholics and French-Canadians alone. Not that I think they are any worse than others, but I am more concerned about them. These signs of moral disintegration are forerunners of revolution. Remember France, ten years, five years before the storm which carried away church and monarchy. Think of Spain, a few years ago.

These portents, I confess, give me more concern, as a father, a Canadian, a Catholic, than the crimes and follies perpetrated in Moscow, or the greater or lesser degree of orthodoxy, heterodoxy or a-doxy in the program of any political party in Canada. In a country like Canada, facts, sentiments and tendencies count much more than theories and doctrines.
This brings me to the third and, by far, the most important basis of social order.
Was it Karl Marx or Lasalle who said that religion is the opium of the people? Like Proud'hon's paradox on property, this also contains a truth and a falsehood. False religion, or religion misinterpreted and misapplied, may, like opium, stupefy and poison an ailing community. But, like opium again, when properly administered, it alleviates sufferings, makes possible an otherwise killing operation, gives sleep and rest, and finally enables the body, individual or social, to recover health and strength.
Religion is not much in vogue these days, -not even among our church-going population in Canada-I mean true religion. Statesmen ignore it, at least officially. Most of the scientists disdain it. Materialists deride it. Nevertheless, it was, it is, it shall remain the only permanent foundation of social order. Without belief in God, in divine justice and mercy, there can be no peace on earth'-no lasting peace between nations, no set order within nations. The brotherhood of man cannot be without the fatherhood of God. No human power has the right to govern men and nations, to command obedience, unless it rests on a God-ordained basis of authority.
Why obey Moses or Caesar, Louis XIV or Henry VIII, Hitler or Mussolini, R. B. Bennett or Mackenzie King, George Henry or Alexandre Taschereau-Heaven knows it is hard at times to obey any one of them!- why, I repeat, obey them unless one believes that all powers, faulty as may be the men in authority, are to them delegated by God through the explicit or tacit consent of the people? Why should I sacrifice some or any of my whims or caprices, still less of my needs, to help any other man unless I believe that all men are the children of the same Father in heaven, redeemed by the One Saviour, Son of God and brother of man?
The essence of religion is the love of God and of one another, and that love must express itself by deeds, individual, social, political, national and international.
Religion cannot maintain its sway on human minds, direct human activities, still less check human greed and all human passions, unless it is taught to man, from childhood to death,

Social Reforms-Mr. Luchkovich
unless it penetrates everywhere-not only in places of worship, but in the home, the school and the shop, in parliaments and in courts of law-everywhere men converse, study, work, govern, legislate and judge. And the teaching of religion, to be effective and enduring, must be given by the duly constituted authority of the church, or under its direction. This is what makes the ever-perplexing problem of church and state relations so difficult to solve in countries like Canada, where several churches are recognized by law and claim, each of them in varying degrees, the right to teach religion in their own way.
On this delicate point, may I be permitted for the first, and probably the last time in this parliament, to confess my faith without equivocation? Born in the Catholic fold, I was reared in a family circle comprising Catholics, Protestants and agnostics. I was exposed to those various currents of thought. Fifty years of study, of travel, of contact with some of the leading minds of our time- and, through reading, of the past as well- have entrenched me in the belief that the Catholic church is the church divinely instituted and divinely inspired to lead men to their eternal salvation along the path of truth and justice, individual and social. Woe to us, bad or tepid Catholics, whose conduct in private and public life stands in testimony against the teaching of the church, a stumbling block to the weak, the unbeliever, the agnostic or the separated brother!
Heaven knows, I wish all Canadians, all men on earth, were true Catholics, better Catholics than I am! But under no circumstance do I believe in conversion by force, or in a state-ordained religion, such as Philip of Spain, Henry VIII in England, Louis XIV or Napoleon in France, Josephus in Austria or Peter the Great in Russia, tried to impose upon their peoples, to the detriment of both church and state.
In our days, all that the church can and does claim in fact is the right to teach, in the home and the school, as freely as in places of worship, the duty of all men to God and to their fellow beings, the respect of legitimate authority, of true liberty also, the practice of justice and charity to all, poor and rich alike. Now, that duty is incumbent upon all churches. Without any sacrifice of principle, dogmatic or ethical, all churches can and should work, either in conjunction or on parallel lines, to help the government and guide the people on their way to social and economic salvation. On the other hand, it is the duty of the state to second the spiritual
power in its mission, but never, never to try and make use of religion for political or party ends.
Mutual help, toleration and forbearance between churches, classes and races, between provinces, cities, towns and rural communities, and also between political parties and factions, are today more essential than ever in Canada, and elsewhere. Without that moral accord, no law, no measure, no plan of financial or social reform, can succeed and save society.
At this point, may I open a short parenthesis and deplore the wave of anti-semitism now passing in the province of Quebec? Launched by a handful of irresponsible individuals, may it soon die out!. It is so unchristian, so contrary to the best traditions of Quebec! -the first part of the British Empire in which the Jews received at the hands of a Frenchspeaking and Catholic majority, twenty-six years ahead of England, the full recognition of their civil, political and religious liberties. Should any French Canadian of sense and understanding be tempted to encourage that propaganda of hatred, let him remember that an attack upon any minority is a threat to all minorities. Jews are in the minority in Quebec, but Catholics and French Canadians are in the minority in eight provinces out of nine. Beware of reactions.
In conclusion may I express the fervent hope that all forces in the land, moral, intellectual and material, will coalesce on a ground of mutual understanding and cooperation to face the present critical situation with fortitude and self denial. Let each and all make his sacrifice to save the nation from the greed and selfishness of too many possessors of wealth and power, and thereby avoid the fast coming revenge of the poor and dispossessed. Let the spiritual overcome the material. Let us all, French or Englishspeaking Canadians, Catholics, Protestants, Jews and Gentiles, raise our souls to heaven and pray the Father of all men and all nations to inspire our leaders in church and state so that they may lead us in the path of salvation. But to accomplish this, they, the leaders, must give to the people who are crying for moral and material nourishment, not the stone of brute force and soulless laws, not empty words of nugatory advice, but the divine bread of justice and the material means to live and let live.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if no other hon. member desires to speak I should like to say a few words before the question is put. The previous speaker (Mr. Bourassa) has introduced

Social Reforms-Mr. Guthrie
a few matters which have been brought to the attention of this house on numerous occasions. He spoke of unemployment, of interest and of other matters. Hon. members in this corner of the house have introduced resolutions dealing with these fundamentals but every time they have been introduced, they have been turned down by the government. Just recently the principle of titles was accepted by the government, and in this connection I have a little plan which may or may not help to solve the present depression, Why not hold the government down to something tangible? It is not the use of titles but the abuse of titles to which this section of the house is opposed.
While the hon. member was speaking I figured out that there were at least seven kinds of titles which could be given to people in this country. A man could be made a duke, a marquis, an earl, a viscount, a baron, a baronet or a knight. I have figured that in Canada there are about ten thousand persons with a hankering for titles. I figure that there must be at least 1,600 with a hankering for the title of duke. If each of these were to pay $50,000 into the coffers of the state it would add to the treasury of Canada about $80,000,000. There are about 1,500 men who would like the title of marquis. At $25,000 apiece, this would add $35,500,000 to the coffers of Canada. About 1,400 would like the title of earl; at $15,000 a head this would make $21,000,000. Thirteen hundred men would like the title of viscount; at $10,000 each this would provide $13,000,000. There are 1,200 who would like to be barons; at $9,000 each this would provide $10,800,000. Eleven hundred would like to be baronets; at $8,000 each, this would provide $8,800,000. There are perhaps 1,000 of the common run of men in this country who would like to have the title of knight; at $7,000, this would provide $7,000,000. Assuming that there are 900 men who would be satisfied with any title; at $6,000 each they would provide $5,400,000. We would thus have the magnificent sum of $183,500,000 to help to balance the budget and solve the question of unemployment and other pressing problems.
I thought that this issue had died away back in 1919; I thought that it had been interred with all the good or bad that there might have been therein, but evidently it has been resuscitated. The Prime Minister has given it a shining badge of honour. I am reminded of a dead fish which has been thrown up by the ocean to rot upon a sandy beach and then taken back again. The whole

thing looks to me like a dead mackerel. I see no reason for reintroducing the question of titles. If anyone wants a title, let him pay for it and provide the magnificent sum of $183,500,000 for the benefit of this country. I cannot express myself in any other words than to say it is like a dead mackerel in the moonlight-the whole thing shines and stinks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT PROPOSING COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO THE STATE OF THE NATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have listened this afternoon to a very able discussion of the affairs of Canada considered on broad and general lines. I am sorry that many members of the government have been otherwise engaged in some of the committees and were unable to remain to hear the greater part of the address of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). He has covered so much ground in his survey of conditions in Canada that it is hard at the moment to express an opinion either favourable or unfavourable in connection with certain of the propositions which he has laid down with his usual force and ability. However, I am satisfied that the house and the country will profit from the clear exposition which he has given of national affairs as considered from his own point of view. I have no doubt that in launching his motion on this occasion it was his intention to place his views fully and forcibly before the house and the country and, the hon. gentleman having achieved that object, I am wondering whether he would now be willing to withdraw his motion or whether he desires the matter to be carried to a conclusion.

speechtext: Will the minister give the house some particulars as to the size of the force at the present time?

When the mounted police bill was

Provision is made in this

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One of their principal
duties is to hold the island formally in the name of the crown. There are some contentious claims in regard to the ownership of it, and I believe that at the present time there is prospect of an expedition under Mr. Shackleton, son of the great explorer, who will go to Ellesmere island within the next few months on a voyage of exploration. The one main object in a few of these very northerly districts is to occupy them formally in possession of the crown.

Is it the policy of the force
to use spotters in connection with the work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; it is not the policy of the force to use spotters.

I am glad to hear the minister say that. I had not intended bringing this matter before the house at this time, but I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the fact that spotters are being used and have been used in the past along the border of the constituency which I represent. I condemn this practice as heartily as the minister does. In connection with narcotics I can appreciate the contention that there may be some reason for it, although even there it is to be deplored. I have personal knowledge however, that spotters have been used, and in the particular instance I have in mind the spotter employed was a boy of twenty, a chap named Campbell from the city of Windsor, who was used to go in and if possible get someone to commit a crime, and the evidence he gave at the police
court in connection with the matter was that he was paid some fifty dollars for the information he would obtain if convictions followed. I stated at that time in the court that I would call the matter to the attention of the minister and I do so now, convinced that I shall have the assurance of the hon. gentleman that the subject matter will be investigated. I have not my file before me at the present moment but I am quite prepared to lay all the facts before the minister and I hope I shall receive his assurance that the matter will be investigated and the practice stopped.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Is it the policy of the department to employ any detectives from private detective firms?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can answer that without a moment's hesitation: no; they have no such instructions.

Are there in the
force to-day people who are carrying on such tactics as were carried on some years ago by Corporal Zanith and more recently by Sergeant Leopold?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Sergeant Leopold was a member of the secret service of the force.

Are tactics carried on by other members of the force similar to those carried on by Sergeant Leopold?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I know nothing in regard to the conduct of Sergeant Leopold for which he should be reprimanded at all. He was carrying out his duty.

I may say that it is commonly believed in a great many labour circles that at ordinary meetings of trade unions and at other gatherings of labour people there are present detectives who are there to work their way into the trade union organizations and on occasion to advise action which would be anything but desirable in the public interest. It seems to me that it is going very far for a government department to have men doing such work as was done some years ago by Sergeant Leopold and as, I presume, is being done to-day. He became an official of an ordinary trade union. As such he undoubtedly had access to the books and he participated in the discussions of that trade union. A trade union is a quite legitimate organization. In talking before labour groups I have again and again been cautioned against listening to certain people who were regarded by the members of the trade unions as spies. Do not, they said, let them lead you to say anything which might in any way give them a tag. I remember meeting Sergeant Leopold ten or fifteen years ago when he was an official of a trade union in Regina. I remember his asldng me to come to his home, an invitation which I could not accept. I thought it was given in all good faith but my time did not permit me to accept it. I think it is an outrageous situation when legitimate trade unions may be invaded by government spies and when we never know whether the discussions that are going on are absolutely in good faith or whether they are being participated in by people who have ulterior motives to serve.
Only the other day I was in a group in Toronto where there had been a good deal of disturbance right within the organization itself and when it was suggested to me that in all probablity one of the men who had provoked the disturbance was an agent of the government. I am in no position to say whether or not that statement was true.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then the statement should not be made here. It is a nasty insinuation against a very good force.
As I say, I am in no position to say whether that statement was true.
Has the hon. member then any right to insinuate that?

Yes, I have because I know the work carried on by Sergeant Leopold and I know the work carried on some years ago by Sergeant Zanith. The latter, it was shown in court, was selling books which he knew to be banned. If instructions were given to those officials to go, if it were possible to do so, into a meeting of the directors of, say the Royal Bank or the Sun Life or the Webster coal combine and secure secrets there, I do not know that I would have very much to say against such action. But when legitimate trade unions are liable to be invaded in this way, I wish to make a decided protest against that kind of thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Then I give a distinct denial to the insinuation which has been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He says that government secret agents or spies have invaded meetings of legitimate trade associations or unions and I give him an absolute denial to that statement. I think his insinuation is unworthy of him. He listens to rumours, rumours coming to him I think in many cases on very questionable authority and his grievance against this particular man Leopold is that he is the one who gave evidence when the eight communists were convicted in Toronto. That is the grievance of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in that instance. I do not know what meetings he attends; I do not know why he has to be warned at those meetings of the presence of spies, but I can assure him that in legitimate meetings of labour unions or associations there are no government agents or spies.
I would be glad to accept that statement of the minister, but I can hardly do so when it was revealed in the statements of Sergeant Leopold that he had been a member of a trade union in Regina.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not say that he was not a member; I said that at that time it was a communist union he was secretary of and at that time he was doing secret service work.
All I can say is that I remember meeting him in the regular trade union meetings in the city of Regina.

Sergeant Leopold was financial secretary or secretary of the local

union of the international brotherhood of paper hangers and painters in Regina and this in my judgment substantiates the statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Whether he may have been placed there to spy on the communists, I have no knowledge, but I know at that time he was an officer of a regularly constituted union in this country. He sat in the Regina convention of the trades and labour congress and if I remember aright, he was some years ago a delegate there at that congress and at the same time, of course, a member of the secret service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This item looks to me as though it were a consolidation of several items as they formerly appeared in the estimates. It covers practically all the estimates of the mounted police.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the same item as that which appeared last year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think there were only two items formerly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Could the minister tell us what it means and could he, say after the six o'clock recess, give us the amounts for the different services represented? As I read the item it does not make much sense:
Pay of force and allowances:	(including
salaries of two constables, Ellesmere island district at $2.25 per diem to assure department against loss through death, arms and ammunition

That is the first sentence. Can the minister tell us just what it means? I think this is a badly compiled arrangement and what would help us in the committee to understand how the total expenditure is made up is to get some details as to the different services that are indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the item is exactly the same as it was last year, but in former years I believe there were two items instead of one. I suppose it was consolidated for the sake of convenience more than for any other reason. I asked the commissioner to be here at eight o'clock; I did not anticipate that the item would be called until then, but I shall have all the details in the evening.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Perhaps we
might take up the next item and pass it, allowing this one to stand.

Before we pass to the next item, I should like to ask the minister whether these policemen in performance of their duty collect fines. For instance, in the enforcement of a federal statute, are the police entitled to go out and say what the fine will be in a particular case and to collect the cash? Have they authority to do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have no authority to collect any fines, but in those cases certain allowances are made under the revenue acts of Canada. I think similar allowances are also made to certain customs officers. These do not go to the men; they go to a trust fund belonging to the force. The individual as such gets nothing of the fine. Formerly a certain amount was paid to the man who gave the information and conducted the prosecution.

I think the minister misunderstood, I am not charging them with collecting the fines in their own interests. I am one of those who support the enforcement of law and order, who will not charge them with anything wrong, but I do think that this excellent body is gradually establishing a custom and system which is bringing discredit on the force and raising a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout the country. It may be the desire to make this one large, grand dominion body; at any rate I know that there are places and operations in which local police, provincial police, and the mounted police are all acting, and the result is productive of public opinion not favourable to good order. Along the front certain regulations and statutes are applicable. For instance there is the law, probably directed against rum running and smuggling, that requires a motorboat visiting the Canadian or the American side to register there, and then immediately return to and register at the nearest customs port. But that has caused a great deal of unnecessary trouble and the imposition of fines upon people along the border. For instance there are two islands in the St. Lawrence, one on the Canadian side and the other on the American. If people pass from one to the other for a game of bridge the boat has to report that it has been over to the other side. That requirement has led
Supply-Mounted Police

to the imposition of fines. Let me tell of one ease that I know will gain the sympathy of the minister and of the committee. Two Americans, a man and a woman, were summering on Wolfe island. They received a notice in the night that their son was in some trouble and that they had to get home immediately. They got a motorboat to take them to Clayton. The man who took them over, a good Canadian citizen resident on Wolfe island, failed to go to Kingston or Gananoque on his return and report that he had been across. One of these policemen went to Clayton, found that this boat had registered there, and that there was no registry of its return to the Canadian side. The result was a fine of 850, with possible seizure of the boat. Now that is inflicting unnecessary trouble and suffering on a man who had done a charitable act. Fortunately we were able to get a certain amount of the fine refunded.
Then there are these house to house searches made on a blanket warrant. There is a long island one mile from the American shore. People there are perhaps eighteen miles from any place on the Canadian side where they might deal. People will not go that distance. A high school boy in Kingston who earns a little money in the summer by rowing Americans, getting the use of a boat from one family and another, was found with a little flashlight that he had purchased on the American side for fifty or sixty cents. He was fined SflS, taking perhaps all his summer's earnings. Another was found with an old pair of overalls, and he was fined $28 or $29. I grant you it is the enforcement of a statute, but it seems to me small pettifogging interference. These people are not smugglers. I support with all my strength the repression of smuggling and rum running but I protest against the police entering citizen's houses with a blanket warrant and with no object in view but the chance of finding small things like that. I say to the minister and to the committee that one of the officials of the Department of National Revenue, Mr. Sim, who has been promoted, said it was rather a raw piece of work. It is not the sort of work that a great body should do.
Let me tell of another case on this island. Two Americans, brothers, had been coming for over twenty years to a certain summer place, not only while it belonged to its present owner, but in the time of his father before him. They had a lot of tackle, a shotgun, a rifle, and other things that had been in their possession for years, ever since they had first gone there. The police came and demanded of the owner of the house

that they be allowed to look around. Remember they were not dealing with highly educated people, and this man did not know what answer to make. They found certain things, one being a paint brush that had been there for twenty years. When he was asked about these articles he was honest enough to tell what had come over from the other side; and having to decide quickly he replied: "They are mine; they were given to me." If he said they belonged to tlie Americans he knew they would be seized. For that he was fined $238. We got a little of it back, but I say to the minister that these things are regarded along the front as petty and unnecessary interference. I do not believe the police should have a blanket warrant to go into the homes of peaceful citizens, not smugglers, not rum runners, and make search from house to house.

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
The house again in committee of supply, Mr. Gobeil in the chair.
Pay of force and allowances:	(including
salaries of two constables, Ellesmere island district at $2.25 per diem to assure department against loss through death, arins and ammunition, barrack buildings, repairs and renewals and furnishings, _ clothing and equipment, communication services, court and legal expenses, criminal investigation branch, enforcement of federal statutes, fuel and light, transport horses and dogs, transport mechanical, dental, medical and hospital, miscellaneous, special services Opium and Narcotic Drug Act,

Supply-Mounted Police
printing and stationery, transport railway, rations, rents, travelling expenses, transport water), $5,603,595.75.

Before six o'clock I had
enumerated a number of cases in the vicinity of the constituency I represent in connection with which I considered there had been unnecessary interference on part of the police. Perhaps I have not stated clearly that near the islands I have mentioned there are farmers who, in some cases, are quite close to the American border, even within a stone's throw, and who, perhaps for weeks cannot reach the Canadian market. Owing to winds, ice conditions in spring and fall and road conditions in winter they are practically separated from the Canadian market. While in some cases I must admit the law has been broken, perhaps the circumstances warranted the action taken. But I do think that the infractions were so small that the police did not have the right to go in and search private houses either on slight or no suspicion, and with very little justification. It may be that there are laws which would make the action of the police legal, but if we have such laws they are causing a great deal of dissatisfaction among people who are living under conditions with which probably most of us are not acquainted. It may have been that some of the officers were inexperienced and new to their work. The time has come however when advice could be given quietly so that the officers would proceed properly. I quite admit that perhaps they should not be instructed to let infractions of the law pass; I would not stand for that. But I do think that they should not have the right to enter a private citizen's house and conduct a search with no authority other than a blanket search warrant, and to state to people who may be quite uneducated that they are operating under a proper warrant.
In about ninety per cent of the houses about which I was speaking the police found absolutely nothing, a point which to me shows that they were dealing with good, law abiding people. In another instance they were dealing with two American brothers who had been in the place in question for over twenty years, both during the father's and the son's ownerships, and who had accumulated quite a number of articles. The son who was in the house at the time of the search and who was approached quickly, inadvertently admitted that the goods belonged to him. He felt that if he said they belonged to the two Americans they would be seized and he would lose two good tourists. For that reason he was fined and the fine was collected. I am asking the minister if the officers had
authority so to act and to collect fines which reached about S250. I am not going to excuse infringements of the law. I must explain however that the other cases I described were of only a very minor nature, one being that of a little schoolboy who had a flashlight worth about fifty cents, and the other being that of a boy who had a pair of overalls.
I believe the minister is sympathetic enough to know that there is dissatisfaction among these people who fear that their homes can be entered by a federal policeman, even though he does not show a proper cause. This condition is raising a great deal of dissatisfaction, and there is a misunderstanding of the conditions under which the people in question are living. As I say, they are twenty miles from Kingston, twenty-two miles from Gana-noque and about fifteen or eighteen miles from the nearest store. I have enumerated all that was found in the search. I believe it is necessary only to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the authorities must not drive the people too far. In these days we are living under peculiar conditions, and just a little bit of what might be termed autocracy among these people will produce a very great deal of dissatisfaction. As I have stated I do not condone any infraction of the law, nor do I excuse smuggling. I am quite agreeable to supporting the law in every way; if the officers know that smuggling is being carried on they should go armed with a proper search warrant. But unless they have a search warrant I say they are not justified in taking action, and the people resent very much the fact that officers can enter private homes and appear to be at perfect liberty to search as they wish. People feel that their homes are their private possessions, and that while in them they cannot be imposed upon. I am aware of the fact that there may be some who may not be in sympathy with what I say, but I know these people and the conditions under which they live, and I do know that there is dissatisfaction amongst them because of this interference for petty reasons. I think it is only necessary to bring the matter to the attention of the minister and those in charge to have a remedy provided. If the law is there, an unjust law, we should be able to amend it. If the law does work an injustice, people should be given some consideration for what has been necessarily imposed upon them by the forces of nature.

I should like to say a word
or two along the same line as that taken by the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross). Those of us who live close to the boundary line have had brought to our atten-
Supply-Mounted Police

May I make a protest to the minister along the same line? My county borders the states of Minnesota and Dakota, and there is a lot of bush in that district. I wish to say at the outset publicly that the officers in my district are about as fine a lot of men as you would want to find anywhere, human and experienced. I do not blame the police. I blame our laws more than anything else. In that bush district, especially during the winter time, a man has to go over to the United States to get his horses shod because he cannot get them shod on this side without going a tremendous distance. So he gets them shod on the other side of the line so that he can haul wood, and suppose he does bring back a few little commodities worth perhaps two or three dollars from the United States. I do not say that he should not have to pay duty on those goods, excise or sales tax, or whatever may be due, but I do say, whether the fault lies with the statutes or not, that the penalty imposed, particularly for a first offence of a petty nature, is too severe, and most of the people living in the district are not in a position to pay the penalty that is imposed. They are not making that kind of money, especially if they are cutting cord-wood. Those who have been cutting pulp-wood in that district have had a very hard time to make both ends meet. Most of them are French Canadians or Norwegians, with large families. They have been receiving a very small price for their cordwood, and there had been practically no sale of pulpwood for the last two or three years until last fall. I would ask the minister to give this matter his serious consideration. A first offender should not be penalized to the extent he is to-day for committing some petty offence. If a man makes a business of smuggling and is

Supply-Mounted Police
caught at it two or three times the penalty should be imposed, but in these petty offences, particularly a first offence, some discretion should be used by the officers because the present penalty imposes a burden on these people. They may be bringing in two or three dollars' worth of goods without any intention at all of defrauding the Canadian treasury. I trust the minister will give this matter his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened with a good deal of interest to the representations which the hon. members for Kingston City (Mr. Ross), Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) have made with regard to the particular districts which they represent in this house. These hon. members fully understand, I would gather from their remarks, that in each of the instances they have related, offences were committed against the customs or excise laws of Canada. As head of the Department of Justice for the time being and as the minister in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police it would ill become me to advise any member of that force to disregard the law. I have to take the other course; I have to give instructions that the laws as they appear upon the statute books must be enforced. If there is anything unreasonable in our customs and excise laws, if there is anything unjusit, if there is anything which should be altered or amended, why not bring in a bill to make the necessary alterations? As the laws stand upon our statute books I have but one duty to perform, and that is to see that they are strictly enforced. There is no discretion permitted to me or to the members of the force in this respect.
I realize the inconvenience and annoyance suffered by people as described by the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross). These people reside close to the border and probably do not think it a very serious matter to break the customs or excise laws of the country in trivial instances. For the information of the hon. member for Kingston I would say that many complaints have been made to the mounted police from business men in Brockville, Belleville and Kingston in connection with the traffic across the river. Because of those complaints, a little greater diligence has been exercised in recent months. One complaint was in connection with the smuggling of motor car radios. Upon investigation it was found that a considerable traffic was going on in these radio sets along lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence river. The former members of the preventive service who have since been transferred to the mounted
police have been instructed to see that there is a strict enforcement of the customs and excise laws. These annoying search warrants, or writs of assistance, of which the hon. member for Kingston complains, have been provided for in the Customs Act for generations. They allow considerable latitude, in connection with the collecting of revenues. They give practically the right of free search of any suspected premises. I realize that in many instances considerable annoyance has been caused, particularly when no evidence of smuggling has been found. I sympathize with these people, but all I can do is to direct the attention of the Minister of National Revenue to the remarks which have been made. Personally, I cannot turn to the right or to the left; I must instruct the police to enforce the laws.
No doubt the hon. member for Lisgar has given his own views in connection with the incident he related. In all probability he knows the parties and he states that, in his opinion, no offence was committed. However, I gather from his remarks that the man was tried before a magistrate of the province of Manitoba and that a fine was imposed for some breach of the law.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understood my hon.
friend to say that he was fined $15.

Under a misapprehension
he pleaded guilty to having the cattle.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A magistrate of the province of Manitoba, over whom I have no jurisdiction, heard the case. The parties appeared before him and a plea of guilty was entered, and I assume the magistrate, in imposing the fine, performed his duty. There was a breach of the law and there was a convic^on. I cannot believe that my hon. friend would expect me to ask the members of the force to close their eyes at an incident of that kind. If the mounted police hew to the line and perform their duties and endeavour honestly to carry out the laws of the country, I do not think they should be open to criticism. They should be commended. If there is anything wrong with the law, then this parliament should alter it but so long as the laws remain upon the statute book, it is the duty of the mounted police to enforce them.

Mr. Chairman, we all admit that the minister is perfectly correct, but we contend that the use of a general warrant of that kind constitutes a misdemeanour. Why should a man who has never been under any suspicion and is known to the whole com-
Supply-Mounted Police

munity as an honest and reliable man have his house searched simply because someone has passed up and down in a boat? Honest people who have had their houses searched and nothing has been found certainly have a grievance. If there is reason to believe that a certain house contains anything, a warrant could be gotten out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They do not require to get a warrant; they have a writ of assistance.
I know they have.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is issued under the Customs Act.

I know just what the criticism would be regarding what I am going to say. The time has long since arrived when people should have some defence against the law. There are too many laws which permit entry into a man's home for the purpose of collecting a tax.
The minister mentioned automobile radios. Police officers went in to collect this tax and valued these sets at S60 each. This set may have been smuggled, but they should have dealt with that matter and not gone back five or six times to close up the man's shop and nearly put him out of business. He had been convicted and had paid a fine and he should have been left alone. This radio set should not have been valued at $60. All along that front you can get one for $23 or $24. These people have every reason to kick against the law. I do not hold the minister responsible but I contend that the home of a man who is above reproach should not be open to inspection at any time the police might come along. All I am asking is that discretion should be used in these cases.
Evasions of the law should be punished, but it is goin^ beyond that when a boy is taxed $28 because of a flashlight. In another case a boy was taxed $28 or $29 for an old pair of overalls. As I said at the beginning, I am not attempting to condone law breaking but I submit that in these cases the law has been too severe. A man who is above reproach in his community should not have his house entered at the whim of the police. If the minister were in my place I know that he would make a similar complaint. I am simply doing my duty and appealing on behalf of a large number of people who feel that an injustice has been done. I do not defend a man who has brought in a radio illegally but, as an hon. member across the way has said, I do think that the penalty imposed in certain cases has been too severe. I submit that a man above reproach should not suffer an injustice such as I have described. We all 
have admiration for British fair play, and we resent anything of this sort. Any man in this house would resent it if a policeman came along, without suspicion, and said, "I am going to search your house." That is all I complain of, and I hope that as a result of bringing the matter forward a little more reason will be exercised. I am quite in accord with what the minister said, that he cannot stand up and say, "Don't do that." I do say however that some exposure, the bringing forward of what is an injustice to some people, will probably result in a rearrangement and some further consideration so that there will be no injustice against good citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The penalties are provided by a statute passed by this house, and I have no doubt that in the case cited by my hon. friend (Mr. Ross) the magistrate took all the circumstances into consideration. I am inclined to think he imposed the minimum penalty.
These matters never came before the magistrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They might have come
before him if the person accused had so desired.
The police simply came in and collected the fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is power in the
officer himself to assess the fine, but that does not prevent the man from going to the magistrate to have it assessed if he desired to do so. I do think that the fines in trivial cases are rather severe under the Customs Act, and I said so last session. There has been a notable modification in the excise penalties. Now, both these acts will be before the house this year, and if hon. gentlemen feel interested in the subject why do they not move amendments when the acts are under consideration, in respect of penalties or of writs of assistance? So long however as these clauses remain in the act the penalties imposed by that act must be paid.

Before recess my right hon.
leader raised a question with the minister as to this vote, which amounts to $5,603,000 odd. It was pointed out that, if not last year, certainly in 1930 this vote was broken up-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Into two pieoes.

And so on. As I say, this is tihe greatest conglomeration of powers and expenditures that one can possibly find embraced within a single pair of brackets. It is true that in 1930 this vote amounted to only $3,000,000 odd, and I grant that since that time we have taken over the preventive service, certain provincial forces, and that warrants no doubt the vote asked for to-night. But in 1930 the item was split up into several subdivisions. We have: Pay of force, including salaries of two constables, Ellesmere island district, at $225 per diem, to ensure department against loss through death, $1,279,772.75. Maintenance, including billeting, travelling expenses, forage, fuel and light, clothing, repairs and renewals, etc., $1,625,452.50. To compensate members of the Roya'l Canadian Mounted Police for injuries received whilst in the performance of duty, $10,000. To assist in enforcement of federal statutes-Expenditure chargeable to this vote shall be in connection with such federal police duties as may be defined by the governor in council upon recommendation of the Minister of Justice-$75,000. To provide for special services in connection with the enforcement of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, $50,000. To compensate William Pinsky for medical attendance on his child, who was fatally wounded by police dogs, at Fort Resolution, $500.
That last item was no doubt for that year alone, but in any event we find that this item in 1930 was split up into five subdivisions. What I think the leader of the opposition objects to, as we all do, is that we have built up a huge machine with very wide powers. I have protested in the past, not perhaps in the house but in public, against the building up of this huge police force with such powers as we gave them last year under the Migratory Birds Act for example, by which they became ex officio game officers, with powers under the Indian Act whereby they act as what I might term truant officers, and with other powers. We have so encumbered this force with positions, with offices and with powers that, as the hon. member for Kingston has rightly said, we have brought the Royal Canadian Mounted 74726-106
Police force into disrepute-a force which we of the older generation were taught in our schools to regard as the greatest institution in the dominion. That institution, I say, has been brought into disrepute by reason of the fact that this government, under the minister, or at any rate with his consent, has allowed other departments to delegate to the force duties that should be discharged by themselves. The vote carries a total of $5,600,000 odd, and we are putting into the hands of the superintendent of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police the power to distribute this vast sum of money as he sees fit. Formerly the amount allotted to the enforcement of federal statutes was $75,000, a sum which apparently was considered sufficient at that time. Now we are leaving in the hands of one man the power to juggle the figures as he sees fit. I think that the minister should reconsider the item. I protested at the time against the added powers delegated to the force and I submit that the minister should now give the committee an assurance that he will recast this vote, not merely from his deputy's books, but with a view to ensuring that one official will not be simply handed a blank cheque to dispose of as he thinks fit. I am asking him to reconstruct the vote so that when we ask him next year how much has been spent in the enforcement of federal statutes he will be able to tel'l us, or how much has been devoted to this or that specific purpose, and so on down the line. In short, I protest giving a blank cheque to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the way here proposed.

Disrepute
nothing. The hon. member for West Lamb-ton (Mr. Gray) says that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has fallen into disrepute. This is the first time I have heard such language used in regard to that force. I have lived for fifty years in the west right alongside them at their headquarters.
The hon. member did not hear what his colleague the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) said about them.

I do not care where he comes from. I heard what my hon. friend said and I want to tell him that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police does not require him or me or anybody else to come to their defence. They have a record of fifty years and it stands good. It is the best record of any police force in the world; I defy the hon. gentleman to go throughout the world and find a police force that has a record equal to that of the Royal Canadian Mounted

Supply-Mounted Police

Police. He says that they should enforce the law with discretion. I have never known them to do anything else. I have been many a time in their detachments; I have associated1 with them in many ways; I have known them as intimately as anyone can and when any hon. member says that they have fallen into disrepute, I want to tell him right now that he and I are at loggerheads.
We always have been.

My hon. friend talks about the boundary. What are we going to do with it? Are we to let United States bootleggers and everybody else in, to commit whatever depredations they please? They did not do it in days gone by and they are not going to do it now.
Will my hon. friend pardon me?

Yes, he
needs pardon, a thousand of them.
While I live on the boundary, I never even mentioned it. The hon. member is again confusing the speech of his colleague the hon. member for Kingston City with mine. Why do they not get together?

My hon.
friend was talking about boundaries and everything else.
May I draw attention to the fact that I never mentioned the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

I never said that the hon. member did. My hon. friend across the floor did so. Let me give an illustration. On one occasion I was going home on a street car in the city of Regina and I was hanging on to the strap as I had to do. A man came up beside me and said, "Hello Doc." I looked at him; I did not know him from Adam. I said, "I have not seen you for a long time." I was fishing. He said, "I have just got home." I said, "Where have you been?" He said, "I have been home for three years." I said, "Where is your home?" He said, "It is in the States. Thank God, I am back in Canada. This is the country to live in, as I tell the people down there every day. I tell them that if they want good government, law enforcement, they have to go to Canada to get it."
That was in 1929.

It has always been the case. For a time in the west we had the provincial police, but now the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are back again and

there cannot be found a finer body of men anywhere; they are the very best. Hon. members do not need to be afraid of the mounted police not enforcing the law properly. If there is anything wrong, the law may be wrong, but that is not their fault; that is the fault of my hon. friend and myself. Let us change the law, but so far as the administration of it is concerned, let us leave it to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and it will be properly carried out.

Before I ask the minister to reply to what I have suggested, may I simply say to the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) that I had and still have the highest regard for the Royal Northwest Mounted Police and if this government or whichever one it was had left the Royal Northwest Mounted Police as such, we would not be debating any such question in this chamber. I hesitate to recall to the hon. gentleman's attention that there is not now any Royal Northwest Mounted Police. I am sorry that that force has been done away with, having been merged in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the estimate for which is now before us and that this force now includes preventive officers, Migratory Birds Act officers and Indian truant officers. That is my complaint, and it is not the subject matter which the hon. member has just mentioned. I am sorry if he does not know the Royal Northwest Mounted Police no longer exists. If he does not, then it is time he consulted the minister whose estimates are now before us.
Why did the hon. member say that the force was in disrepute?
I am merely discussing the item that is now before the committee, not what may have happened in the past.
What is the difference between the two forces?
Simply that there is no Royal Northwest Mounted Police force.
What is the difference between the new force and the old?

There is a very big
difference.
What is it?

The hon. member need only consider the men to whom we were accustomed, the big policemen we had in w'estern Canada. They are now a thing of the past.

Supply-Mounted Police

I think the minister understood the point I tried to make as regards the splitting up of the vote so that we might have the details. He has always been fair in connection with the matter. Perhaps I am wrong and if I am I shall be glad to be convinced. I have expressed my view and I would appreciate hearing his.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to giving the details for which my hon. friend has asked, but I emphatically disagree with him when he says that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have fallen into disrepute. It is a more efficient force to-day than it ever was in the history of the country. It is a better recruited force. The same physical standards are maintained now as have been in effect since the force was first established. There has been no change in that respect. As the years go by, it will no doubt increase in efficiency; experience leads to efficiency in those respects, but in every sense it is a better force to-day than ever it was before. It remains the finest police force in the world. The fact that some new duties have been cast upon it, not with the idea merely of increasing its duties but with the idea of saving a great deal of money to the people of Canada-
That is a matter of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the reason the migratory birds convention and the customs preventive service Were placed under the mounted police. The arrangements for this last transfer were made by the former government, as the Minister of National Revenue would state were he in his seat now.
The vote itself is in the same form this year as it was last, but the leader of the opposition wanted some details. In former years there were two or three subdivisions of the vote. I may state roughly it is estimated that the mounted police force costs about S2,000 a man or a little more, but the whole of this vote is not lost to the treasury of Canada. About SI.500,000, or perhaps a little better, comes back into the treasury, not into the hands of the department or of the mounted police force, but into the consolidated revenue fund. So the net cost would be in the neighbourhood of $4,000,000 and not the $5,600,000 which we ask for in the estimates.
The largest item is that of pay and allowances, which was set out as a separate item in the year referred to by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) the amount for pay and allowances this year is $3,549,159.49. The next item is that of maintenance, which amounts to $2,054,436.26. Those two items
make up the whole amount of the appropriation for which we ask. As regards pay and allowances, I suppose I do not need to describe this item in greater detail; it represents just what it says, the pay of the force and allowances to the force. The maintenance includes a great number of miscellaneous items. The main items I will give, in round figures:
Rentals throughout Canada.. ..$201,000
Rations for the force	110,000
Uniforms and equipment	 227,000
Transport	  818,000
The amount for transport is made up of four items, as follows:
Water transport, which includes the operation of the marine,
that is the customs service.. ..$315,000
Railway transport	 175,000
Mechanical transport	 275,000
Horses and' dog transport	 53,000
Total	$818,000
Mechanical transport includes the cost of motor cars; we have about 400 cars and trucks. Formerly this was a mounted force, but it is not so to-day in the former sense. In the early days they had 600 or 700 horses, but now I think there are just 240 horses. Ex' perience has demonstrated that horses are not fast enough for modern police work. The modern criminal, the hold-up man, is equipped with a fast motor car, and if he is to be overtaken and arrested the policeman must be equipped with a car capable of equal speed. Therefore in trucks and cars we have about 400 all told. These cars average about three years in service. After they have gone from 35,000 to 45,000 miles and break down we turn them in and get an allowance on them on a new car. Of course the cost prices of the new cars are standard prices; the competition is as to who will give the largest allowance on the old cars.
The other items are:
Hospitalization	$ 60,000
Civil service salaries	 160,000
Headquarters civil service	 32.000
Criminal investigation department. 61.000 Printing and stationery	 100,000
We have a considerable staff of civil servants throughout the dominion. Then in
addition there is a long list of minor items which you might call sundries or contingencies.
After submitting the matter to the treasury board and after consultation with the comptroller of the treasury it was decided to put this whole vote in one item. It was formerly in one item, but it was subdivided into five
Supply-Mounted, Police

sections as stated by my hon. friend. One of those items, that for compassionate allowances, will not appear in the future because the amendment to the act passed last week will provide for that. The Narcotic Drug Act is now under the heading of criminal investigation, amounting to $61,000, formerly $75,000.
A separate vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, it is included in this item; it is all one vote. The Narcotic Drug Act vote is wiped out altogether and is now under the general vote for maintenance; there is no special allocation for the drug act enforcement.

This is but another example of the usurpation of power by this government, although perhaps this is the most aggravated case. It is no use for the minister to tell us that this one vote contains all those items. I am disturbed when he tells us that the comptroller of the treasury, in consultation, I presume with the commissioner of police and himself, has agreed to a sum of $5,615,000 being lumped in one vote. Parliament does not know of and can have no control over the disposition of those moneys. The minister tells us that certain allocations are made; that is true as far as departmental allocation goes, but if there is a deficit on any one of these allocations then it is very convenient for the minister or his commissioner to take money from some other item; parliament has no control. The hon. minister knows perfectly well the reason these votes were subdivided; it was that parliament could have control over the particular vote. Under the former administration there was no possibility of taking a sum from another vote and using it for any vote that was short. But here the government and the commissioner may use their discretion in regard to the whole $5,615,000; they may switch these votes in any way they like.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, no.
Perhaps the comptroller of the treasury has something to do about it, but parliament has nothing to do with it, and formerly parliament did have that control.
An awful difference in view!

I should say there is. This is not the only instance, but it is the most aggravating one. It is going on in practically every department of the government. Take the Northwest Territories vote, or take the one with which I am most

familiar, the Mines Department; they have all been lumped since this government came into office. For the purpose of getting the estimates through the house I will admit it is a good system as far as the government is concerned, but a bad one from the point of view of parliamentary control. When parliament passes them item by item the government as the servant of parliament cannot spend more than the amount allocated under each item, but when the whole sum is lumped the department has a free hand, subject only to the comptroller of the treasury. I have not examined that act very carefully, but I wonder if the comptroller of the treasury will not allow the commissioner and the minister to spend this $5,615,000 for the various items set out without reference at all to whether or not they are keeping within the items given to parliament as making up the amount. If they are voted as separate items, then neither the minister nor any one else can spend any more than the amount allocated unless they secure a warrant for the purpose, which they have to have voted when parliament is convened. The complaint I make is that in all these votes as they have been lumped during the three years this government has been in office, control over the expenditure of public moneys is taken away from parliament. My complaint is not about the administration of the mounted police force; I do not know anything about it; I presume it is being efficiently managed. But not only in this particular vote but in half a dozen other votes the same thing has been done. In the Indian department you see nothing allocated for the maritime provinces, for Ontario, for Quebec- no; it is all lumped in one sum, and the minister and the department can spend that sum without reference to the allocation that formerly existed under specific votes. The government takes a much wider power than parliament ever intended the minister to have. I register now my protest against this system that is gradually taking from parliament the power to control expenditures by votes in the House of Commons.
