Will the estimates which the
minister has given with respect to the various details, namely fuel and light, air services and the other services he has outlined, be
maintained, and will no vote or any part of it be transferred to another department? Will the minister give that undertaking to the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I give that undertaking as far as I am able to do so. These figures are all appropriated, have all been examined by the treasury board, and been included in one item.
But that is not my complaint. The minister is too old a parliamentarian not to know that he has full authority over the $5,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have given the undertaking, and if I am still in office I shall carry it out.

I am not
questioning the minister's good faith, but I am saying to him that votes which formerly were under separate headings and voted for specific purposes are now lumped in one sum. I am not saying that this is the only example. We could turn to the Department of Indian Affairs and find items in one lump sum. I am merely pointing out to the minister and to the committee that there has been a continual usurpation of the powers of parliament, and a tendency to give to the minister the right to spend willy nilly money which formerly had been allocated to separate votes which could not be exceeded. That is my complaint.

Under this item I should like to ask three questions. A few moments ago the minister spoke about the high standard of recruited men. I Should like to know how recruits are chosen, because in the eight years I have attended parliamentary sessions not a single young man from my section of the country has been able to get into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, although there have been many applications. I know that at the present time when there are so many men out of employment it would be a difficult matter for a new recruit to find his way into that wonderful police force, but I should like to learn from the-minister as to what recruits are chosen, or what' their qualifications must be. I do not know the exact number of police on the force, but there must be hundreds of them, and if appointments were divided among the 245 constituencies some young men would be chosen from every section of the country. I believe the applicants from my section are typical of our fine young Canadianism, and I should like the minister to enlighten me on this subject.
Sv/pply-Mounted Police

The second question I wish to ask is this: Is it true, as is currently stated in northern Ontario, that there is no direct communication between the headquarters of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at Ottawa and the officers of that body in the arctic zone, and that the only direct communication is through American channels? I pointed out only a few days ago to the acting Minister of Fisheries that if such an anomaly existed it should be remedied at once.
In the third place, I should like to compliment the government for their innovation of two years ago when they gave to the guards around the parliament buildings the big fur coats to be used during the winter months. I believe those coats are made from buffalo pelts, and I should like the minister to tell the committee if the supply is to be extended to all members of the force. I repeat that it was a worthy act. To have those men standing throughout cold nights in the winter months, practically freezing to death, was most unfair, and I should be in favour of issuing the coats to every member of the force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to the last point taken may I say that we are endeavouring to supply all members with these fur coats made from Canadian buffalo hides. I believe in a very short time we will have accomplished the full issue.
In regard to the question about recruiting, may I say that the force is at the present time a trifle over-recruited. There is a wastage in all forces of this kind, and every few months some vacancies occur. The allotment throughout Canada is made by provinces, having regard to the number of men operating in each province. We try to keep our proportions constant, and it is quite possible that when the applicants to which the bon. member referred filed their applications there were no vacancies in the Ontario contingent. When application is made a very critical examination, as to natural intelligence, education and physical development, is given. Any man who passes the examination is then placed on the waiting list, and as vacancies occur they are filled from that list. I may tell my hon. friend that I do not myself see the application lists; that is a matter with which I am not in any way personally concerned. When, on occasions, applications come to me from hon. members, I refer them at once to the commissioner who, in turn, with his subordinates, deals with them without reference to or consultation with me in any respect. I do not know about the applicants to which the hon. member referred, but if he will let me

have their names I shall make inquiries and make a report as to how they stand.
As to communications, may I say that we have direct communication by radio through Canada with all the important Arctic stations, but in two or three of the minor and more remote stations we are able to obtain communications only through American stations in Alaska. That condition we hope to remedy some time in the near future. I may say however that we have direct communication now with all important points.

What is the practice in renting quarters for the mounted police? For instance, let us consider the town of Bathurst in which there is a property under rental for the police. What is the practice and how is it worked out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have a great many
rented quarters throughout Canada. The practice is to look over the particular locality where we desire quarters and to ask the district officer commanding in the neighbourhood to make inquiries as to suitable quarters and as to rentals. When he has done so he makes a report to the head in that particular province, and that report comes forward to the commissioner at Ottawa. After an inquiry as full as we can make it, we select the quarters.

The reason I ask the question is this. The police headquarters in Gloucester county are in the town of Bathurst. They were very suitable quarters close to the business centre of the town and to the post office. Considerable expense was incurred on those quarters, I do not know whether by the proprietor of the property or by the police department. The property was rented from one named Lee Palmer, and the police continued to occupy those quarters during a period of a year or perhaps two. But all at once word came for a change in the location and the police were moved to almost a back part of the town. It has caused considerable talk and all kinds of rumours as to why the change was made. I would like to have the reason why the property rented from one Lee Palmer was discontinued as police headquarters in favour of the property mow occupied. The minister may not be in a position to give that information offhand, but if he will have it looked up I shall be glad to get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall see that it is looked up as speedily as possible, and I will write my hon. friend giving him the information

Supply-Mounted Police

Although I quite appreciate what the minister lias said, I was rather surprised when he stated a few moments ago that the physical standards of the mounted police had not been changed since the force was first established. Probably no force in the entire service of His Majesty the King enjoyed the reputation of the northwest mounted police. When the queen's jubilee was held in 1897 the finest body of men that attended that celebration from any part of the empire was the detachment from the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and at any gathering of British military units since the mounted police have maintained the same high place. It requires no praise from me to uphold their fame and their reputation for efficiency in this Canadian country. They established a record in western Canada before this country was opened up which certainly has never been surpassed at any time or place. But what I rose particularly to say, and it is not by way of criticism at all, is that when I was a much younger man than I am now I spent a number of years on the western prairies and frequently came in contact with these men, and the surprise that I got to-night was to hear the minister say that the physical standards have not been changed for admission to the force, because at that time the force was composed of big men. I do not ever remember seeing in those days a man in the northwest mounted police who was not able to look down on the top of my head without any difficulty at all. They were splendidly built, manly fellows. I have met many of them in western Canada whose parents had sent them out all the way from India to join the force just for the excellent training they would receive, but I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, there are a great many men in the force to-day who are not tall enough to look down on the top of my head.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Five feet eight inches is the minimum.

That lets me out, then. I do not propose to criticize the present standard at all because I believe it is recognized in police circles the world over that the smaller man is the more active and more efficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Hear, hear.
Oh, oh.

I merely wish to make that observation. While I am on my feet I should like to say that it has been stated

a number of times by the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross) that the members of the mounted police are authorized to collect penalties for infractions of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Just the customs law.

It may be that in the wisdom of the department that is the correct thing to do, but it seems to me that if there are not actual openings for abuses in that regard, certainly the people who are guilty of the infractions are not getting the fairest show in the world. If they were brought before a magistrate all the circumstances of the case would be considered and the fine adjusted to fit the crime, so to speak; but if there is a specified penalty for every infraction of the customs law I presume the mounted police must exact it, and, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Kingston to-night, there are a great many cases in which the penalty fixed is entirely too severe.

There is not a specified fine, but the officer is supposed to ascertain the value of the smuggled article, and as I pointed out in the case of an automobile radio that is not by any means the end of it because in that case they took three times the value of the article. There is no specified fine, but there is a principle to be observed. The officer I suppose has to go back to the customs and get the value of the article. That is the principle on which they told me they had acted. I may be wrong and if so I should like to be corrected.
They must have applied the dump.
Yes, and after they have ascertained the value, there is a fine of twice that amount.
I should like the minister to state whether he thinks it is a reasonable and proper state of affairs that these constables should be permitted to collect the fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to express any opinion in regard to the Customs Act, the administration of which is not in my department. If I were to give my own opinion I think the penalties under the Customs and Excise Acts are too severe; but they are there, and until they are altered I do not know that I can do anything but enforce them.

I want to
protest again, as I have done on former occasions, against the constable who lays the complaint having the right to impose the fine.
Supply-Mounted Police

That did prevail in the old territorial days, but now that magistrates are much more conveniently located and easy of access it does seem to me that the constable who makes the arrest and files the complaint should not have the right to impose the fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I just want to explain that. It is an erroneous impression that the constable who makes the arrest can try the case or impose the fine. He cannot do it in any part of the country. Under the Customs Aot the man who makes a seizure has the power to impose a penalty. I agree with what the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has said with regard to a constable making an arrest and then imposing a penalty. I will go further and say that I have always been of the opinion that the magistrate who issues an information should not try the case concerned. He hears one side of the story when he issues the information and his mind is apt to be made up before he tries the case. In many remote districts this would not be possible, but in general it should be the practice followed.

I was in the revenue department for a number of years and on many occasions I have made use of the writ of assistance. In my opinion it is very seldom that an officer using this writ will do what is not right. There are cases where this happens, but such cases are the exception. An officer, like every other human being, is liable to err in judgment, but my experience has been that the responsibility for any injustice done, especially in connection with the fines imposed, lies upon the shoulders of the magistrates. We sometimes see a magistrate imposing different fines for the same offence. He will try a case one day and impose a fine of -S200; a similar case will come up the nekt day and a fine of only $100 will be imposed. How is this done? The magistrate consents to the charge being brought under another section of the act where a lesser fine can be imposed. In that way favouritism is shown and the police officer is blamed instead of the magistrate.
I agree with the minister that a magistrate who takes a complaint should not try the oase. When he receives the case his mind is liable to be made up from the story given by the complainant. When he tries the case the next morning he may hear a different story but his mind has been set by the story he heard the day before. The same magistrate should not try the case except in special instances when there should be two magistrates.
[Mr. C. A. Stewart

Reference has been made by hon. members on both sides to the high standard of our mounted police force, but there seems to be some change of sentiment in this regard. I suggest to the minister that the hiring out of large numbers of the force to different provinces has not been conducive to the maintenance of the high standard of this organization. This force has rightly had a high reputation in the northwest. The minister will remember the matter in connection with which we had a conversation a few days ago. When this force was formed it was never the intention that it should be hired out to provincial governments and I am convinced that such procedure is not in the best interests of the force.

What is the position in
connection with the administration of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act? Is any headway being made in the mitigation of the opium and narcotic evil?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The provisions of the
act, as regards the suppression of the habit, are being carefully followed out with the assistance of the mounted police. There were 340 prosecutions last year for various infractions. I am asked whether there is any amelioration. I do not think it is very pronounced. There is a certain improvement, but not very considerable, though the indications are rather favourable. There is still much room for improvement in this respect.

Have many actions been
taken against the legitimate trade, pharmacists and medical men, in connection with the opium and narcotic drug traffic?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Last year one medical
man was prosecuted. There are a number of instances in which they are warned and counselled, so that the one prosecution does not indicate the full activity; but in view of the peculiar conditions that exist they proceed with discretion, and the medical men who are on the doubtful list are carefully observed and supervised. As regards the pharmacists, there were no prosecutions during the year.
They are all good.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No, I do not say that
exactly, but they are supervised. Their books are inspected at regular intervals to see that they conform to the law and that their sales are recorded in the proper way.

Has the minister considered
what took place in British Columbia last year in regard to the growing of poppies? Out there the growing of poppies has become rather extensive and there were some prosecutions of Hindus and others who had been baking the heads of poppies, drying them and rsing them in some form or other. It is of particular interest to us in that province to know what the attitude of the government is, whether the department has examined the
poppy heads to ascertain how much opium they contain and, in view of the fact that they do contain a little opium, whether restrictions will be placed on the growing of poppies.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The matter is receiving consideration. I cannot make a definite statement at the moment but my memory is that the question of suppressing the cultivation of the poppy in this country is now being considered.

Speaking of opium and narcotic drugs, it used to be the practice of the authorities in Canada a few years ago

and I know what I am talking about-to send around certain men, whether you call them spotters or stool pigeons or by any other name, to the medical men. Not infrequently it happened that a hard looking individual would turn up at the office of a medical man -an individual who very evidently was an opium addict, who very evidently was suffering and badly in need of relief; and with a great deal of persuasion, occasionally the medical man would be prevailed upon to give him, not a prescription for a narcotic, but some temporary relief. Fortunately I was never one of those medical men, and I am not speaking for myself, but I thought at the time that the practice was contemptible, because shortly afterwards the medical man concerned would be taken to task if not actually fined for what he had done. I rise merely to express the hope that it is no longer the practice of the department to carry on that form of campaign. I should like the minister to make a statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The practice of using these men as decoys-
Decoys, precisely.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: -is not made use of by the department. I believe it was formerly, although I have no personal knowledge.
It certainly was.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: At any rate, others in connection with the department before my time, as well as myself, have disapproved of instigating infractions of the law and then proceeding to punish the persons concerned. That procedure does not exist to-day.

In a current issue of a magazine called Health, I read in an article these two short paragraphs:
Those interested in the health movement in Canada have felt that it is most important that the principle of dominion leadership in health matters be maintained if we are to ultimately develop a coordinated health
Supply-National Health

program for the dominion and that the most important unit in such a program should be the dominion Department of Health. Any weakening of this department would appear to be a serious matter.
Therefore the announcement of a few weeks ago that the division of child welfare which had rendered admirable service for more than ten years under the distinguished direction of Doctor Helen MacMurchy had been dissolved and its functions turned over to one of the voluntary associations, came as a distinct shock to everyone interested in the progress of public health in Canada.
Evidently the division of child welfare, which m-ost certainily had been doing excellent work in this country and for the federal government, has been discontinued. Might I inquire of the minister what led up to the discontinuance of this really excellent branch? It is a well known fact that Doctor Mac-MurChy was one of the most able physicians in the entire dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The work as carried on by the division of child welfare within the department has been transferred to an organization called the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare.
That is a voluntary organization, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes. Far from there
having come to my notice anything in the way of criticism, a very large number of letters have been sent to me personally commending and approving this change. It has been remarkable how from all parts of the country there have been expressions of approval of the change. All the former objectives of the division of child welfare are now being carried out and, I believe, more effectively and efficiently by the organization to which this work has been transferred. As the change has occurred within only a comparatively few months, one is not justified in speaking of actual results and experience on the basis of a few months' operation. On the other hand, so far as the work has gone under the new organization, the result is promising. If the change does not prove a success, it can be altered again, but the change was not made on the basis of there being any doubt of its being a success. There is, however, still the alternative that should the new method not be satisfactory, the former procedure can easily be restored, but that is not what I am looking for as the result. The name of the secretary of this voluntary organization under which the work is now being carried on is, I think, familiar to all hon. members, especially to those who are interested in social welfare, Miss Charlotte Whitton, who is very active

and efficient and who is familiar with conditions throughout the country. In the arrangement which we have made with this organization there is a special provision that its committee shall have on its board two medical men in Ottawa, one who is a specialist in obstetrics, and the other a specialist in connection with children's ailments and diseases. They are there as advisers to the council. In addition, Doctor Heagerty, director of the medical health branch of this department, is also a member of the council and in cases where advice is required or sought, it is given by this committee of an obstetrician, a pediatrician and the head of our own health service who has the diploma of public health. One advantage of the change is that those who are engaged in the work come into closer contact with the people than was the case with our division of child welfare previously. The Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare has branches throughout the country and therefore is able to come into intimate contact -with all centres. Nothing but good will come from its work and the principles of social welfare and health and the care of maternity cases and children will be brought to the people more widely and in a more intimate way than has been the case in the past.
As regards publications, the Department of Health issued from time to time suitable pamphlets for the instruction of mothers and families. This is not being discontinued, but it will continue to be carried on by the organization which I have mentioned and there will be the advantage of the articles being reviewed and approved by the specialists of whom I have spoken and who are now engaged by the year for their advice and instruction.
Is the government making a grant to this Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The previous grant was $10,000; with the ten per cent cut it may have been $9,000. We are now paying about $12,600 to the council. There is considerably less expense under the change than there was previously.
Is this the only voluntary association of this type that is receiving a grant from the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I see that last year we gave this organization, the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare, $9,000; previously it had been $10,000. Then there is a grant to the Canadian National Committee for Mental Hygiene.

This year?

Supply-National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This year. These are the most akin. There is a grant of $18,000 to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind; a grant of $22,500 to the Canadian Tuberculosis Association; a grant of $9,000 to the Victorian Order of Nurses; one to the St. John Ambulance Association, and one to the Red Cross.

Does the minister think it is good business to delegate to a social organization the functions formerly performed by the department in connection with child welfare? The Department of National Health is a comparatively new department under this government, and I understood at its inception, that its purpose was to give leadership to the social agencies all through Canada that were doing health work. It is true there are departments of health in the different provinces, but I understood that this department was to lead and coordinate the efforts of all the health organizations. To me as a layman this change seems a step in a backward direction. I know from my experience in the Department of Immigration that when we delegated the functions of the department to organizations for the purpose of bringing immigrants into the country it only led us into difficulties. I protest against this move; I do not believe it is good business to delegate to a society, headed by Charlotte Whitton or anybody else, the functions formerly performed by the Department of National Health. I think the minister will find that as time passes too much power will be usurped by an organization of this sort. It is all very well to say that the chief health officer of the department sits in as a member of the board, but he will be entirely overshadowed. Moreover, constant requests will come from this organization for further assistance. It seems to me that the national health is important enough to require that this department should retain the powers with which it was clothed, in regard to child welfare as well as other activities. I take it that child welfare is one of the most important functions of the department. I do not know much about this council, it may have great merit, but I assume it is much the same as other organizations of the kind, and to hand over to it the powers and authorities formerly held by the department to my mind is a step in the wrong direction. I regret that the minister has taken it, and I protest against such a policy.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I think perhaps the hon. member was not in the chamber when I gave the reasons for what is being done, because I
believe that if he had heard what I said he would not be so strong in his opposition. However, I recognize the right of different people to hold different views. I believe it is a step in advance; he believes it is retrograde. Within a year or so we shall see who is right. I ask the members of the committee to bear it in mind and see which prophecy proves nearer to the truth.
My hon. friend says that the director of the health division will be overshadowed; I think he does not know him. From my experience I do not believe he will be overshadowed; either the whole affair will proceed satisfactorily and in the interests of the country, or it will not be continued. It is well safeguarded by the two specialists I have spoken of, who are here and available every day to advise the association. The work instead of being curtailed will be considerably enlarged and extended.
It will be if you pay for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Excuse me; that is not borne out by the facts. There is a saving in expenditure rather than an increase.
If my hon friend will allow me, if he lives long enough-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: May I continue, Mr. Chairman? I shall be glad to give my hon. friend an opportunity in a moment. At the present time there is an economy as far as expenditure goes.
There always is at the start.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is entitled to hold a different view. But I think there is a very great deal to lead us to believe that by this change there will be a gain in efficiency in looking after maternity cases and children and social conditions.

I wish to support the criticism of the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) regarding what we might call this division of labour by the Department of National Health. I cannot understand why the care of child welfare was taken from the department. I am sorry that having to be away from here at a committee meeting to-night I did not hear what the minister said earlier in the evening, but it seems to me we are not making nearly enough of our federal health department. I admit that there is a health department under each provincial government, but in my opinion a great deal of work could usefully be done in coordinating the activities of the different
Supply-National Health

provinces through the central agency. It seems to me that we may as well do away with the department entirely, if it is not going to be any more aggressive than it has been in the last three or four years. Without spending a great deal more money but with much more activity we could help the provinces. At the present time one hardly ever hears of anything being done by the federal department, and as the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) has said, I feel that in turning child welfare over to a private institution a mistake has been made.

A few moments ago the
minister mentioned the name of Miss Charlotte Whitton. I was going to ask him if it was due to this lady's influence that the change had been made so that the federal department of health had discontinued activity in child welfare and had transferred the work to this voluntary organization known as the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare. I understand Miss Whitton is secretary of this institution, and it is reasonable to ask if her influence had anything to do with the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I would not like to
suggest anything of the kind with regard to a distinguished lady such as the one in question. Perhaps the question was not asked seriously; I hope not. I know that those who are connected with the federal council were willing, the department was willing, and arrangements were therefore made.

A short time ago the
minister told us that the federal government was making grants to institutions connected with mental hygiene, the blind, child welfare, tuberculosis, the Victorian Order of Nurses, the Red Cross and the St. John Ambulance Association. One very beneficial organization, the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, has not been considered in this grant. True, its activities deal only with venereal disease, but that disease is one of the greatest menaces to the health of our people. It seems strange that all the organizations named should be honoured with assistance from the federal government but that no assistance should be given to the very active organization I have named. Further than that, the federal government have withdrawn the $200,000 grant from the provinces, and there is probably no other medical organization throughout the length and breadth of the land that means so much to the welfare of our people as does the movement to exterminate venereal disease. May I suggest to the minister, in view of the fact that so

many organizations are receiving assistance, that the grant should be extended to this very laudable movement, and that they may be empowered to proceed with a work which in many parts of the country has been temporarily discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have listened carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden), and I admit that if it were possible to give assistance to this organization it would be quite proper. Indeed, other organizations might be included in the list, which I do not regard as by any means exhaustive. The organizations were included through selection more than anything else. I should like to draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the operations of the Canadian Social Hygiene Council are not entirely restricted to venereal disease. They deal with all forms of disease.
But chiefly with venereal troubles.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That may be, but the fact is that the council deals with all forms of public health measures; I have learned that from the officials. Some years ago $200,000 was voted, and later reductions were made, first to $150,000 and then to $100,000. I wish to point out however that the vote was not given to the social hygiene council.
It was given to the provinces; I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes, the vote to the provinces has been discontinued.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
While I do not wish to advise the association as to what it should do, because that is a matter which must be left to their own judgment, I have said to their officials that it would be better for them to restrict their work to venereal disease. I believe there is advantage to be gained in concentrating on something of an important and definite nature. I must admit that the Canadian Social Hygiene Council is not on the list I have named; I should be pleased if it were. I should not like to encourage the idea of applications for grants from other sources. The object of giving the $200,000 originally was to give a start to the movement throughout the provinces, also with the hope that once it was operating and was seen to be an effective measure the provinces would be able to carry on. It may be that the work is being carried on to a lesser degree, but good work is still being done.

Supply-National Health

I wonder if the minister realizes that by the very fact of cancelling the grant of $50,000 to the provinces, he is destroying the only connecting link that existed between the federal government and the departments of health in the various provinces. Two years ago when we discussed this question and begged the minister to reestablish that grant, he stated that he would take the matter under consideration. I wonder if he would not take under consideration this year the desirability of providing in the supplementary estimates the sum of $50,000 for this purpose. I know that the departments of health in the various provinces, more especially in the province of Quebec, were depending absolutely on the portion they were receiving of that grant of $50,000 to carry on their special services, on venereal disease, for instances, as mentioned by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden).
There is another question which I would ask the minister to consider. He stated a moment ago that he had transferred certain duties to a special body in Ottawa which seemed, so far as I could judge by the minister's statement, to act in the main locally in Ottawa, and perhaps in Ontario. I wonder if the minister has taken the trouble to inquire what has been done in the province of Quebec.
Last year I called the minister's attention to the fact that the province of Quebec had adopted a different system from any other province so far as child welfare was concerned. Ten years ago what they call sanitary units were organized under the direction of one who is now the superintendent of health in the province of Quebec, Doctor A. Lessard. The movement was started in the county of Beauce, and the results there, so far as child welfare was concerned, were so marvellous, that it spread until at the present time we have in the province fifty-five sanitary units, each with a medical officer paid by the provincial government, and in the unit, when it embraces more than one county there are two or three nurses who are also paid by the local government. They are given an allowance to enable them to operate all through the summer, and they visit not only the principal centres in each county, but even the most remote sections. They give lectures on hygiene and prevention. They visit every family in each community. They advise mothers and instruct them in the precautions to be taken in case of isolation, and so forth. They teach them what precautions to take against infectious diseases, and give instruction on all other subjects
relating to hygiene. These units have been operated by the province, and the only contribution which the province receives in support thereof is $12,000, which is subscribed by the county itself, the remainder being paid by the government.
So far as venereal diseases are concerned, if the minister will take the trouble to read the last report on public health issued by the province of Quebec, he will discover that we are practically depending entirely on the grant received from the federal government to carry on the campaign against venereal diseases.
As to tuberculosis, we have adopted in the province of Quebec, over and above the care of the people affected with tuberculosis, the system prevailing in France called the Granger system. It has also been adopted in England and in parts of Scotland. It consists of segregating from contaminated families in the big centres the children of families who are not affected by the disease. They are placed in the country under the supervision of the parish priest, and are visited daily by the officers of the health unit. Of course the system is expensive. It costs nearly $20 per month to maintain each child, and the whole of that expense is borne by the provincial government. What surprises me is that in view of all these new methods that are being adopted all over Canada, the federal department of health has never taken the trouble to ascertain through the college of surgeons of the different provinces what method could be adopted to coordinate the work done in the provinces with that which is being done by the federal department of health. It seems to me that the federal department should take the lead in this matter, and that it should first of all ascertain through the different medical colleges what could be done to improve the situation. Then reports can be received from the provinces, and if you had a conference with the provinces on public health it seems to me that you would arrive at much better and more material results than you have to-day, under the haphazard method that is now being followed of transferring over to famous ladies or others the duties of the department in regard to public health.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have listened with great pleasure to the views put forward by my hon. friend from Rimouski, who has advocated with much vigour several very excellent things. It is particularly gratifying to me that he has done so because he has advocated the cooperation that has been carried on by the department for a number of years. We recognize that the health units
16S4
Supply-National Health

have prospered and done very excellent work in the province of Quebec, and we are pleased that that is so. It is to their credit; but it is also their duty. That is the idea of the whole health organization in this country, that the provinces should do this work, and I think that it can be said that the province of Quebec has led in the matter of health units. Why? Outside of the characteristics of the people of the province of Quebec-
Because they had a good minister.
And a good government.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I think one of the main reasons is that their clergy have supported that movement and encouraged their people to have confidence in it, a.nd so the health units have been conspicuously successful in the province of Quebec.
My hon. friend from Rimouski said that the provincial government had been the basis and support of that work. He does not recall perhaps that the Rockefeller Foundation, if my memory serves me, gave a substantial grant for a certain number of years to support the initiation of these health units. That grant may have ceased; I rather think the time has elapsed.

No, they are still
subscribing.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They still are. Well, I ;hink it would be fair to mention that to the members of the house.
I have no objection whatever. I praise the movement.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The Rockefeller Foundation has been a rather generous benefactor. I am delighted that my hon. friend from Rimouski has advocated another thing that we are doing. Please do not forget that we have a very useful coordinating and cooperating organization called the Dominion Council of Health, which meets twice a year in Ottawa. I believe the next meeting will be in June, and I ask all those who are interested in health matters to attend the meetings and see what it is all about. The council is composed of a health representative from every province, a representative of the agriculturists, a representative of Labour, and two from the women's organizations. A specialist from the Toronto university also attends, in addition to one of our own officials. At these meetings, which last two or three days, an effort is made to coordinate the work of health officials throughout the dominion. Notes are compared and when considered advantageous, there is a standardization of records and statistics 
relating to the treatment of infectious diseases and all such matters. Matters of interest and value to health officials are discussed. The dominion tries to take the lead in health matters, and, speaking in a very modest way, I think we have taken that lead. This organization is called together at the expense of the federal government and papers are read and discussed. I do not think there is anything which could prove more useful and valuable. A small pamphlet on health is published and distributed to the medical men throughout Canada. Many of them write in and say they are delighted to have it. This is another method of coordinating public health matters in this country. In any consideration of these matters I do not think we should omit mentioning the Dominion Council of Health.

After listening to this
discussion I have come to the conclusion that if we go much further the only thing we will have left is the name. In my opinion, the minister has not yet given a reason for the abolition of the child's welfare department and the delegation of certain powers to an outside organization. I have not been convinced that this change was necessary and I should like to know why it was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I have gone over this
matter twice already, but apparently the hon. member was not in the chamber.
I was present.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I shall be pleased to
go over it once more. We believe that there has been a gain in efficiency and an increase in activities by reason of this change.

Do I understand from
that that the department was inefficient prior to the change being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No, but there are
degrees of efficiency and I believe we have added to the efficiency. In any case a change would have been necessary because the director of child welfare had exceeded the limits of the requirements by two years. Even apart from that reason, I believe this change will be in the interests of the people of Canada. As far as child and mothers' welfare matters were concerned, the department could not come in actual contact with the people, but this condition is now being corrected. The new organization is not divorced entirely from the department. The senior officer of our health division is a member of the council and a member of the committee, and with him are two others, one an obstetrician and the other a specialist in child diseases. These

Sup-ply-National Health
gentlemen advise the council and supervise its work here in Ottawa. The publications which were formerly published by the department will still be published by the new organization in an improved form.
As I said before, this new method may be discontinued at any time. Hon. members need have no apprehension that we are bound to carry it on forever, but I do not anticipate that there will be any request for a change back to the old method. Our object is to pursue this matter in the best way possible and that could not be done under the old arrangement. The department could not reach the people to the same extent as this council will be able to do. They have branches from one end of Canada to the other and will be more closely in touch with the homes of our people. If our aim is to educate and help the people, I believe this organization offers the best method of doing so.

How much was saved
by this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The expenditure last
year for salaries, travelling expenses, printing -we did a good deal of printing in the way of pamphlets-and stationery, amounted to $19,217.99. For this year we estimate the salaries at $6,165; travelling expenses at $358.85; stationery and printing at $1,818.51, making a total of $8,342.36. That is the estimate I have here but I do not think it is quite accurate; I believe the expenses will be about $9,500.

Do I understand there
will be a saving of about $10,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The saving will not be
anything like that. I gave the figure for last year, $19,000 or a little over. Under the new arrangement, allowing for the grant, and some additional expenses, I would put it at $13,500 as my estimate.

It might be as well for
us as a committee actually to realize and to understand what an important change such as this will mean, and the only way we can do so is to have it indicated by the minister what the activities of the former child welfare department of the federal health department were, and what activities are contemplated by the Canadian Council on Child and Family Welfare.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The activities are the
same. The advantage I believe is that they will be carried out in a broader and more extensive way.
The minister has said on several occasions to-night that the federal department of child welfare did not come in contact with the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No, I did not say that; I said, not to the same extent. I say so many things that are changed just a little bit, not intentionally, but they are changed. I did not say that they did not come in contact with the public; that is impossible. I said that they did not come in contact, nor could they come in contact, to nearly the same extent as they will under the new organization.

I have one question to
ask with reference to item 194, which deals with the important matter of national health. In regard to the administration of the acts respecting opium and narcotic drugs, may I ask the minister whether the jurisidction of the department has been confined to the enforcement of these acts in Canada or whether extraterritorial jurisdiction has been exercised by the department outside the dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
As far as the actual
work goes, being instrumental in taking steps to suppress the traffic, the efforts are entirely within Canada; prosecutions naturally are within Canada. But our sphere does extend beyond Canada, to this extent, that we send our special narcotic official to Geneva, generally once a year, to take part in the deliberations there and to assist in the drawing up of regulations regarding the restrictions and suppression of narcotics.

That means, then, that
there is international cooperation with respect to these acts?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Oh yes, quite so.

The minister has called
attention to the fact that the department has saved about $10,000 in making the change, taking the work of child welfare away from his department and turning it over to a private association. He informed the committee that better work is being done and that more people are being helped through this change. I would ask, therefore, where was money wasted in the earlier arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: First of all, I did not say $10,000. I think the figures will show about five thousand five hundred.

I think the saving is between $5,000 and $6,000.
Supply-National Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks
where money was wasted. I am pointing out where the saving will be.
But where did we waste money before?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In the department there was a medical director besides four stenographers. That expense was maintained and is now eliminated, because the organization is now being carried on by the council on child and family welfare.

Did four stenographers
make up the difference of between $5,000 and 86,000? At that rate they are paid more than most stenographers.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have not the exact figures; they have not been finally adjusted. I say however that there is a saving because there will be a lesser expenditure of several thousand dollars, I presume, about five. But I do not wish to make an exact statement. There will be less expenditure of some thousands of dollars under the new arrangement.

I would ask a question with regard to the taking away of the grant from the Canadian Social Hygiene Council. The minister admits that some excellent work has been done by this association. Personally I do not know of any health association in Canada that has done more and better work across this dominion. It has probably been a very important link connecting up the work of the health department in the various provinces. Up to a few years ago they were getting a grant of $100,000. The minister himself admits the value of this association and the good work they have done. I understand that the grant has been entirely discontinued for two years. Why was it discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They never had a grant of $100,000.
How much was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That grant went to
the provinces, not to the social hygiene council.
Can the minister give the exact amount that did go to the social hygiene council?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The last grant given a few years ago was $10,000, although it had been larger than that. There is naturally a little confusion about the grant that has been going to the provinces and administered by them, but the last grant to the social hygiene council was $10,000.
Considering the excellent work that association has done, will the minister inform the committee why the grant was taken away?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I know nothing about these terms; I did not use the word excellent. I said it was a good organization.
What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I said that there was
a selection of them and all the organizations unfortunately are not receiving grants. Further, I would like again to point out that social hygiene does not restrict itself to venereal diseases and I presume that were there a grant to-day, it would again go to the provinces where it is concentrated in dealing with that disease. The social hygiene council, so far as I am aware, deals with all conditions of ill health.

The minister has stated
once or twice in the course of the debate that the federal department of health was coordinating the health services of the provinces through the medium of the Canadian health council, and I think he said that this body met once or twice a year-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Twice.

-to discuss matters and that through their deliberations and activities, the activities of the various provinces in health matters were coordinated. Some years ago I had the pleasure of attending one of the meetings of that body, and if I remember well, it discussed a wide variety of subjects, all no doubt pertaining to the health of the Canadian people, but, as I understand the situation, at that time those papers were merely read and discussed and possibly some recommendations were passed on to the federal health department. I was not able to see from their activities that they would have any possible influence on the health services of the provinces. If we are going to give the citizens of Canada a uniform, standardized policy of health, we require a statutory control exercised by the federal government through its health department. We must have a standardized control with the nature and degree specified of the activities of the provinces with regard to health services to their citizens. In order to get that, I am of the opinion that the federal government will have to contribute to the expense of such a program, because undoubtedly it will entail considerable expense. I do not think we shall ever have an entirely satisfactory health program in Canada until we have such a

Supply-National Health
coordination of the services of the provinces, and we can have a definite coordination only through statutory control exercised by the federal government. So far as the Canadian health council is concerned, although, as I stated before, I have attended one of its meetings, I cannot see that it can have very much influence on the health services of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
There again we do not hold the same view. My opinion very clearly is that it exerts a valuable measure of cooperation, bringing together the health officers in the different provinces and others interested in that work. The result is just the same as one would have in a conference -the benefit of an opportunity to discuss matters with one's fellow health officers. There is no question that it is of much value.
I should like to make this statement on the subject generally; those who have been speaking have been pointing out matters to be criticized and suggesting improvements. [DOT]One might gather from that that public health in Canada is not advancing. That is an incorrect impression. I have not heard one member either to-day or yesterday referring to the marked advance being made in Canada every year. I can speak for my own province that had the first minister of health in Canada.
The first in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Perhaps in the world. This gentleman was formerly, I think, a minister in the cabinet of the hon. member for Gloucester. I refer to Doctor Roberts, [DOT]who was, I certainly was under the impression, the first minister of health in Canada and I daresay, as the hon. member for Gloucester says, the first minister of health in the world.
Let us consider for a moment the case of Hew Brunswick, because I think we can learn a good deal from that little province. Public health there has advanced steadily; it has kept pace with the progress of similar systems anywhere else. Let me now refer to Ontario. Without making undue comparisons, I think Ontario stands at the top, so far as public health in Canada is concerned. Is there no improvement there? Why, it is striking. All I ask is that we do not have the impression and that the impression does not go out to the public that we are not gaining ground steadily. The same thing applies to the other provinces; Quebec and the others are doing excellent work. I have no doubt the degree of improvement has varied in different provinces according to their means and perhaps
for other reasons, but the fact is that public health is from year to year gaining substantial ground in Canada, notwithstanding the objections advanced with regard to leadership and organization.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister, the committee and especially the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) to the fact that the little province of Prince Edward Island has had a minister of health since 1927.
I might state for the information of the hon. member that New Brunswick was the first province to have a separate department and minister of health and that department was established in 1918.
I bow to the superior wisdom of the hon. member.

We have had remarkable figures given for the province of Quebec with regard to the work being done under the full time health units. It is well recognized that the establishment of these health units was made possible through the generosity of the Rockefeller Foundation. I understand that foundation gives grants, probably one-third of the cost, for the first three years and then withdraws its support. A number of provinces have hesitated to develop that sort of health care because of the fear that when the Rockefeller Foundation stops its grants, the provinces and the municipalities could not afford to continue the work. I should like to congratulate most heartily those who have been carrying on the work in Quebec, because it has been productive of splendid results. I believe British Columbia comes next in the number of full time health units. Alberta has two experimental units. Recognizing the fact that the Rockefeller grant is for only three years, I would ask the minister whether he has given thought to the matter of asking the government through his department to continue the grant when the support of the Rockefeller Foundation is withdrawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Unfortunately the hon. member was not in his seat when we were discussing the Rockefeller grants and these health units of Quebec that had done so well. As to the hon. member's question, I do not wish to indicate any expectation that it will be carried on this year.

Has the minister given sufficient thought to the matter to cause him to advocate that the federal government take the responsibility of carrying on where the Rockefeller Foundation leaves off? If that is done I am sure other full time health units would be established throughout Canada.

Supply-Pensions

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I quite understand that it would have to apply to all parts of the country; it could not be restricted to one province. AH I can say is that we will make a note of the matter and look into it and consider it further. But I do not wish to give any assurance in that regard. Anything done would have to apply to all the provinces.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Pensions payable to men on active service, Northwest rebellion 1885, and general pensions, and civil flying, $22,000.
Will the minister explain the reduction of $4,000 in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The amount is based on what was expended last year. It chiefly concerns those who were in the Northwest rebellion, and that was a good many years ago.
What is the number of these pensioners left now?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The amount expended last year was $21,510.78; slightly less than the vote for this year. There are 49 disability pensioners and 6 dependent pensioners, a total of 55. For the Northwest rebellion these are the items: 23 privates, 1 corporal, 1 sergeant, 1 warrant officer and 1 lieutenant, a total of 27; and 1 dependent. Then there are a few others, for instance one under civil flying. When members of the civil service fly on duty-which is quite seldom, I understand- they would come under this. There is one such case.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

Wednesday, March 21, 1934
